paragraphs: What does terraform destroy actually delete?

Every resource recorded in the state file for that workspace and configuration. It does not touch resources created outside Terraform, and it does not touch other workspaces or other state files. The destroy plan is shown for approval first, and reading it is worth the time. The count of resources is the quickest sanity check that you are pointed at the environment you think you are.
How do I preview a destroy without actually destroying?

terraform plan -destroy produces the destroy plan without executing it, and -out saves it for review. This is the safe way to answer "what would go away", particularly before tearing down anything shared. In CI, generating a destroy plan and posting it for approval is the equivalent of the normal plan-then-apply flow.
How do I protect resources from accidental destruction?

Add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to anything holding data. Terraform then refuses any plan that would destroy it, including a full terraform destroy, and you must remove the flag deliberately to proceed. Combine that with provider-level protection, RDS deletion protection, S3 bucket versioning and MFA delete, so a mistake has to get past more than one gate. Note prevent_destroy cannot stop a destroy triggered by the resource being removed from configuration entirely.
Can I destroy just one resource?

Yes, with terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.example, but treat it as a recovery tool rather than routine practice. Targeting operates on a subset, so the rest of your configuration is not reconciled and dependent resources may be left referencing something gone. A cleaner approach for permanent removal is to delete the resource from the configuration and run a normal apply, which Terraform plans with full dependency awareness.
What is the difference between terraform destroy and deleting resources in the console?

terraform destroy removes the resources and clears them from state, leaving everything consistent. Deleting in the console removes the resources but leaves state believing they exist, so the next plan shows Terraform intending to recreate them, which is drift, and at best confusing, at worst a surprise recreation of something expensive. If resources were removed outside Terraform, use terraform state rm to bring state back in line.
Should terraform destroy ever run automatically in CI?

Only for genuinely ephemeral environments. A per-pull-request preview stack that is torn down on merge, or a nightly cleanup of a sandbox account. Even then, scope it tightly with a separate state file and credentials that cannot reach production, so an error in the pipeline cannot destroy the wrong thing. For anything long-lived, destruction should require a human.

terraform-destroy.markdown:
## What Is terraform destroy?

`terraform destroy` removes all infrastructure resources managed by your Terraform configuration. It is the opposite of `terraform apply`.

```bash
terraform destroy
```

Terraform reads your configuration and state file, calculates a destroy plan (everything that exists gets removed), shows you the plan, and waits for approval before deleting anything.

> **Warning:** `terraform destroy` is permanent. Deleted cloud resources cannot be recovered unless you have backups (e.g., RDS snapshots, EBS snapshots). Always review the destroy plan carefully.

## The Destroy Plan

Before destroying anything, Terraform shows you exactly what will be deleted:

```
Terraform will destroy all your managed infrastructure, as shown below.
These resources will be destroyed in the proper reverse order.

  # aws_instance.web will be destroyed
  - resource "aws_instance" "web" {
      - ami           = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0" -> null
      - instance_type = "t3.micro" -> null
      - id            = "i-0abc12345def67890" -> null
      - public_ip     = "54.123.45.67" -> null
    }

  # aws_security_group.web will be destroyed
  - resource "aws_security_group" "web" { ... }

  # aws_subnet.public will be destroyed
  - resource "aws_subnet" "public" { ... }

  # aws_vpc.main will be destroyed
  - resource "aws_vpc" "main" { ... }

Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 4 to destroy.

Do you really want to destroy all resources?
  Terraform will destroy all your managed infrastructure.
  There is no undo. Only 'yes' will be accepted to confirm.

  Enter a value: yes
```

Notice the **reverse dependency order**: Terraform destroys in the reverse of the creation order. The EC2 instance is destroyed before the security group, which is destroyed before the subnet, which is destroyed before the VPC. This prevents dependency errors (e.g., you cannot delete a VPC that still has running instances).

## When to Use terraform destroy

| Use Case | Appropriate? |
|---|---|
| Tearing down a dev/test environment | â Perfect use case |
| Cleaning up after a tutorial or experiment | â Perfect use case |
| Removing a feature branch environment | â Standard practice |
| Decommissioning part of production | â ï¸ Use with extreme caution + backup strategy |
| "I'll just recreate it" in production | â Almost always wrong |

`terraform destroy` is most commonly used for ephemeral environments, dev environments, feature branch previews, CI/CD testing environments, and tutorial cleanup.

## Partial Destroy with -target

To destroy a single resource (or module) without touching the rest:

```bash
# Destroy a single resource
terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.web

# Destroy an entire module
terraform destroy -target=module.database
```

Terraform will show a destroy plan for only the targeted resource:

```
  # aws_instance.web will be destroyed
  - resource "aws_instance" "web" {
      - id = "i-0abc12345def67890" -> null
    }

Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
```

> **Caution:** `-target` can leave your state inconsistent. If other resources depended on the destroyed resource, they still exist in state but their dependency is gone. Always run a full `plan` after a targeted destroy to check for consistency.

## Auto-Approve in CI/CD

Like `apply`, you can skip the confirmation with `-auto-approve`:

```bash
terraform destroy -auto-approve
```

This is commonly used in CI/CD pipelines to automatically tear down ephemeral environments:

```yaml
# GitLab CI, destroy on branch delete
teardown:
  stage: destroy
  script:
    - terraform init -input=false
    - terraform destroy -input=false -auto-approve
  when: manual
```

## Preview the Destroy Plan Without Destroying

To see the destroy plan without any risk, use `terraform plan -destroy`:

```bash
terraform plan -destroy
```

This is functionally equivalent to `terraform destroy` without the actual deletion, great for reviewing what would be destroyed before committing.

## The destroy Lifecycle Hook

If you want certain resources to be retained even when the configuration is removed, use the `prevent_destroy` lifecycle argument:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "critical_data" {
  bucket = "my-production-data"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}
```

If you try to destroy this resource (or remove it from your config), Terraform will error:

```
â·
â Error: Instance cannot be destroyed
â Resource aws_s3_bucket.critical_data has lifecycle.prevent_destroy set to true.
â To allow this object to be destroyed, remove the lifecycle block or set
â prevent_destroy = false.
âµ
```

Use `prevent_destroy` for critical resources like production databases, S3 buckets with important data, or any resource where accidental deletion would be catastrophic.

---

## terraform fmt, Format Your Code

While you have your terminal open, `terraform fmt` is a command you will use constantly:

```bash
terraform fmt
```

It automatically formats all `.tf` files in the current directory to match the Terraform style guide, consistent indentation, aligned `=` signs, and proper spacing.

```bash
# Format and show which files were changed
terraform fmt -diff

# Format all files recursively (including modules)
terraform fmt -recursive

# Check formatting without making changes (useful in CI)
terraform fmt -check
```

Example, before formatting:

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
ami = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"
instance_type = "t3.micro"
  tags = {
    Name = "web-server"
  }
}
```

After `terraform fmt`:

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  tags = {
    Name = "web-server"
  }
}
```

> **Pro tip:** Add `terraform fmt -check` to your CI pipeline. If anyone submits unformatted code, the pipeline fails, this enforces consistent style across the team without manual code review comments.

---

## terraform validate, Validate Your Configuration

`terraform validate` checks your configuration for syntax errors and internal consistency:

```bash
terraform validate
```

Successful output:

```
Success! The configuration is valid.
```

Error example:

```
â·
â Error: Unsupported argument
â   on main.tf line 8
â An argument named "instanse_type" is not expected here.
â Did you mean "instance_type"?
âµ
```

`validate` catches:
- Syntax errors (missing braces, typos)
- References to undeclared variables or resources
- Invalid attribute names for a resource type
- Type mismatches (e.g., passing a string where a number is expected)

What `validate` does NOT check:
- Whether the cloud credentials are valid
- Whether the AMI ID exists in your region
- Whether the VPC ID actually exists
- Anything that requires calling cloud APIs

```bash
# Typical workflow before pushing code:
terraform fmt -recursive
terraform validate
terraform plan
```

---

## Knowledge Check

<MCQExercise

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does terraform destroy actually delete?**

Every resource recorded in the state file for that workspace and configuration. It does not touch resources created outside Terraform, and it does not touch other workspaces or other state files. The destroy plan is shown for approval first, and reading it is worth the time. The count of resources is the quickest sanity check that you are pointed at the environment you think you are.

**How do I preview a destroy without actually destroying?**

`terraform plan -destroy` produces the destroy plan without executing it, and `-out` saves it for review. This is the safe way to answer "what would go away", particularly before tearing down anything shared. In CI, generating a destroy plan and posting it for approval is the equivalent of the normal plan-then-apply flow.

**How do I protect resources from accidental destruction?**

Add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` to anything holding data. Terraform then refuses any plan that would destroy it, including a full `terraform destroy`, and you must remove the flag deliberately to proceed. Combine that with provider-level protection, RDS deletion protection, S3 bucket versioning and MFA delete, so a mistake has to get past more than one gate. Note `prevent_destroy` cannot stop a destroy triggered by the resource being removed from configuration entirely.

**Can I destroy just one resource?**

Yes, with `terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.example`, but treat it as a recovery tool rather than routine practice. Targeting operates on a subset, so the rest of your configuration is not reconciled and dependent resources may be left referencing something gone. A cleaner approach for permanent removal is to delete the resource from the configuration and run a normal apply, which Terraform plans with full dependency awareness.

**What is the difference between terraform destroy and deleting resources in the console?**

`terraform destroy` removes the resources and clears them from state, leaving everything consistent. Deleting in the console removes the resources but leaves state believing they exist, so the next plan shows Terraform intending to recreate them, which is drift, and at best confusing, at worst a surprise recreation of something expensive. If resources were removed outside Terraform, use `terraform state rm` to bring state back in line.

**Should terraform destroy ever run automatically in CI?**

Only for genuinely ephemeral environments. A per-pull-request preview stack that is torn down on merge, or a nightly cleanup of a sandbox account. Even then, scope it tightly with a separate state file and credentials that cannot reach production, so an error in the pipeline cannot destroy the wrong thing. For anything long-lived, destruction should require a human.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a variable, a local and an output in Terraform?

An input variable is supplied from outside the configuration, by a tfvars file, the command line, an environment variable, or a parent module, and is how the same code serves different environments. A local value is computed inside the configuration and cannot be overridden externally; it exists to name derived logic and avoid repetition. An output exposes a value outward, either for a human to read after apply or for a parent module to consume. Variables flow in, locals stay internal, outputs flow out.
What is the precedence order for Terraform variable values?

Lowest to highest: the default in the declaration, then TF_VAR_ environment variables, then terraform.tfvars, then *.auto.tfvars files alphabetically, then -var-file on the command line, and finally -var, which beats everything. Precedence applies per variable, so a tfvars file that sets one value leaves the others at their defaults. When a value is not what you expect, printing it through terraform console is the quickest way to find which layer supplied it.
How do I keep secrets out of my Terraform configuration?

Do not put them in tfvars files that are committed. Mark the variable sensitive = true so it is redacted from output, then supply the value through an environment variable or a CI secret, or better, read it at plan time from AWS Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store or Vault with a data source, so it never exists in a file at all. Remember sensitive only hides values from console output; they are stored in plain text in state, which is why state encryption and access control matter regardless.
Do I need a tfvars file for every environment?

It is the common and workable pattern: dev.tfvars, staging.tfvars, production.tfvars, selected with -var-file. Keep them in version control so environment differences are reviewable, and keep secrets out of them. The alternative, separate directories per environment, each with its own backend, gives stronger isolation because credentials and state can be scoped separately, and is worth the extra structure once production is involved.
When should I use a local instead of a variable?

When the value is internal logic rather than something a caller chooses. A name prefix built from other variables, a map of common tags, a computed CIDR. All locals. If a person deploying would reasonably want to set it differently, it is a variable. A frequent mistake is making everything a variable, which produces modules with twenty inputs where three would do and makes them unpleasant to use.
Why can't I read a value from inside a module without an output?

Because the module interface is deliberately a contract. A parent module can only see what a child explicitly exposes through output blocks, which is what lets a module change its internals without breaking callers. If you need a value from a module, add an output for it, and when writing a module, expose anything a caller might plausibly want, since adding an output later is easy but callers have no way to work around a missing one.

terraform-variables-and-outputs.markdown:
Three constructs move data through a Terraform configuration, and choosing the right one is most of what makes a configuration readable.

| Construct | Direction | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| **Input variable** | In | The caller: tfvars, CLI, environment, parent module |
| **Local value** | Internal | Computed inside the configuration |
| **Output value** | Out | Returned to the caller or read after apply |

The rule of thumb: if someone deploying needs to choose it, make it a **variable**. If it is derived logic you want to name once, make it a **local**. If something outside needs to read it, make it an **output**.

## Input variables

```hcl
variable "environment" {
  description = "Deployment environment"
  type        = string

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be dev, staging or prod."
  }
}

variable "instance_count" {
  description = "Number of application instances"
  type        = number
  default     = 2
}
```

A variable with no `default` is **required**. Terraform prompts for it interactively, which in CI means a hung pipeline unless `-input=false` is set.

Always write a `description`. It is what `terraform-docs` renders and what a colleague reads instead of your source.

### Types

`string`, `number`, `bool`, plus collections, `list(string)`, `map(string)`, `set(string)`, and structural types:

```hcl
variable "subnets" {
  type = map(object({
    cidr = string
    az   = string
    public = optional(bool, false)
  }))
}
```

Typing an object rather than accepting `any` turns a runtime failure deep inside a resource into a clear type error at plan time. `optional()` with a default keeps the interface small for simple callers.

### Validation

`validation` blocks are underused and cheap. Rejecting a bad value at plan time with your own message beats a provider error three resources later that names nothing useful.

## Passing values in

Five mechanisms, evaluated lowest to highest precedence:

| Source | Precedence |
|---|---|
| `default` in the declaration | Lowest |
| `TF_VAR_name` environment variable | â |
| `terraform.tfvars` | â |
| `*.auto.tfvars`, alphabetically | â |
| `-var-file` on the command line | â |
| `-var` on the command line | **Highest** |

Precedence is per variable, so a tfvars file setting one value leaves everything else at its default.

```bash
terraform apply -var-file=production.tfvars
terraform apply -var="instance_count=5"
export TF_VAR_environment=staging
```

For real projects, keep a tfvars file per environment in version control, as long as it holds no secrets. That makes the configuration reproducible and the values reviewable.

## Secrets

Mark the variable sensitive and supply the value from outside:

```hcl
variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
```

`sensitive = true` redacts the value from plan and apply output. **That is all it does.** The value is stored in plain text in state, so state encryption and access control remain the actual protection.

Better still, do not pass secrets in at all. Read them at plan time from a secret manager:

```hcl
data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" {
  secret_id = "prod/payments/db"
}
```

The value then never exists in a tfvars file, a CI variable, or anyone's shell history.

## Local values

Locals name internal logic. They cannot be set from outside, and they are computed once per run:

```hcl
locals {
  name_prefix = "${var.project}-${var.environment}"

  common_tags = {
    Project     = var.project
    Environment = var.environment
    ManagedBy   = "terraform"
  }
}
```

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "artifacts" {
  bucket = "${local.name_prefix}-artifacts"
  tags   = merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "artifacts" })
}
```

The common-tags pattern is the most valuable use: one place to change your tagging convention, applied everywhere.

Locals can be overused. A configuration where every literal is indirected through a local is harder to read, not easier. Reserve them for values used several times, expressions complex enough that a name helps, and anything you expect to change.

## Outputs

```hcl
output "bucket_name" {
  description = "Name of the artifacts bucket"
  value       = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
}

output "db_endpoint" {
  value     = aws_db_instance.main.endpoint
  sensitive = true
}
```

Outputs do two jobs. They surface values to humans after an apply, and, more importantly, they are the **only** way a module returns anything to its caller. A parent module cannot reach inside a child to read a resource attribute, so anything a caller might need must be an output.

```bash
terraform output                # everything
terraform output bucket_name    # one value
terraform output -raw bucket_name   # unquoted, for shell interpolation
terraform output -json          # machine-readable, for scripts
```

Note that `sensitive` outputs appear unredacted in `-json`, so avoid printing the whole document into a CI log.

## Explore further in this section

| Sub-topic | What you will learn |
|---|---|
| [Input Variables](/tutorials/terraform/terraform-input-variables) | Types, validation, tfvars and precedence in depth |
| [Local Values](/tutorials/terraform/terraform-local-values) | Expressions, functions and common patterns |
| [Output Values](/tutorials/terraform/terraform-output-values) | Module interfaces, sensitive outputs, CI usage |

## Quick reference

| Task | Syntax |
|---|---|
| Declare an input | `variable "name" { type = string }` |
| Reference it | `var.name` |
| Declare a local | `locals { key = expression }` |
| Reference it | `local.key` |
| Declare an output | `output "name" { value = ... }` |
| Read an output | `terraform output name` |
| For a shell script | `terraform output -raw name` |
| Pass a file | `terraform apply -var-file=prod.tfvars` |
| Pass one value | `terraform apply -var="key=value"` |
| Environment variable | `export TF_VAR_key=value` |

---

## Final Thoughts

Variables in, locals for internal logic, outputs out. Most unreadable Terraform comes from blurring those lines. Parameterising things that never vary, or computing in-line what should be a named local. Keep the required variable surface small, give everything a description, and remember that `sensitive` protects logs rather than state.

sections.title: What Are Terraform Input Variables?
paragraphs: Terraform input variables are named values that let you parameterize your infrastructure code. Instead of hardcoding settings like AWS region, instance type, environment name, or subnet CIDR ranges directly into resources, you define variables and then pass values into them when Terraform runs.

Think of a Terraform module like a function in a programming language. A function becomes reusable because it accepts parameters. Terraform modules work the same way. Input variables are the parameters of your infrastructure code.
Without variables, you might write something like this:
This works, but it is rigid. If you want a staging environment that uses t3.small, or a production environment that uses t3.medium, you have to edit the file itself. That is fragile and inconvenient.
With variables, the configuration becomes reusable:
Now the same code can be used in development, staging, and production by passing different values.

sections.title: Why Use Input Variables?
paragraphs: Terraform input variables solve several real-world problems for DevOps teams:
A single configuration can be reused in different environments. For example:
Hardcoded values scattered across resources are hard to maintain. Variables pull those decisions into one obvious place.
Instead of editing .tf files every time a value changes, teams can provide values using .tfvars files, environment variables, or CI/CD pipeline secrets.
If you create modules later, variables become the public interface of the module. A good module clearly defines what callers can customize.
Variables let you describe expected inputs, enforce types, and reject invalid values before Terraform touches real infrastructure.

sections.title: Declaring Variables with variable Blocks
paragraphs: A Terraform input variable is declared with a variable block:
The label after variable is the variable name. You reference it elsewhere using var.<name>.
A well-defined variable block usually contains at least description and type, and often default if the value should be optional.

sections.title: Required Variables vs Optional Variables
paragraphs: A variable is required when it has no default value.
If you run Terraform without providing a value, Terraform will stop and ask for one, or fail in automation.
A variable is optional when it has a default.
If the caller does not supply a value, Terraform uses false.

paragraphs: A map stores key-value pairs of the same value type.

sections.title: object
paragraphs: An object groups multiple named attributes, each with its own type.
Objects are excellent when related settings belong together.

sections.title: tuple
paragraphs: A tuple is an ordered sequence where each position can have a different type.
Tuples are supported, but they are less common in beginner Terraform code. In many cases, an object is easier to read because attribute names are clearer than positional indexes.

sections.title: Variable Validation Blocks
paragraphs: Type constraints are useful, but sometimes they are not enough. A value can have the right type and still be invalid.
That is where validation blocks help.
If someone sets environment = "qa", Terraform fails before making changes.
Validation is one of the simplest ways to make Terraform safer for teams. It turns vague mistakes into clear, actionable errors.

sections.title: Assigning Variable Values
paragraphs: Declaring a variable only defines the interface. You still need a way to provide actual values.
Terraform supports multiple input methods.

sections.title: 1. terraform.tfvars
paragraphs: If a file named terraform.tfvars exists in the root module directory, Terraform automatically loads it.
This is convenient for local development or small demos.

codeBlock.code:
project_name  = "billing-app"
environment   = "dev"
instance_type = "t3.micro"
instance_count = 1

sections.title: 2. *.auto.tfvars
paragraphs: Any file ending in .auto.tfvars or .auto.tfvars.json is also loaded automatically.
These files are useful when you want separate environment-specific values.

codeBlock.code:
# dev.auto.tfvars
project_name  = "billing-app"
environment   = "dev"
instance_type = "t3.micro"

sections.title: 3. -var flag
paragraphs: You can pass individual values directly on the command line:
This is useful for quick experiments, but it becomes hard to manage when many variables are involved.

codeBlock.code: terraform plan -var="environment=staging" -var="instance_count=2"

sections.title: 4. -var-file flag
paragraphs: You can explicitly tell Terraform which variable file to load:
This is a common pattern for different environments:

codeBlock.code:
terraform plan -var-file="dev.tfvars"
terraform apply -var-file="prod.tfvars"

sections.title: 5. Environment variables with TF_VAR_
paragraphs: Terraform also reads environment variables prefixed with TF_VAR_.
The variable name after TF_VAR_ must match the Terraform variable name.
This is especially useful in CI/CD pipelines because secrets can be injected from the platform instead of stored in files.

codeBlock.code:
export TF_VAR_environment="prod"
export TF_VAR_instance_type="t3.medium"
export TF_VAR_db_password="SuperSecretPassword"
terraform apply

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I pass values to Terraform variables?

Several ways, and they combine. A terraform.tfvars file is picked up automatically, as is any *.auto.tfvars. Pass a specific file with -var-file=production.tfvars, a single value with -var="region=eu-west-1", or set an environment variable named TF_VAR_region. For real projects, keep values in a per-environment tfvars file under version control, as long as it contains no secrets, since that makes the configuration reproducible and reviewable.
What is the order of precedence for Terraform variables?

From lowest to highest: the variable's default, then environment variables prefixed TF_VAR_, then terraform.tfvars, then *.auto.tfvars in alphabetical order, then -var-file on the command line, and finally -var, which wins over everything. Later sources override earlier ones on a per-variable basis, so a tfvars file setting one value leaves the rest at their defaults.
How do I handle secrets in Terraform variables?

Do not put them in tfvars files that get committed. Mark the variable sensitive = true so its value is redacted from plan and apply output, then supply it through an environment variable, a CI secret, or, best, a data source that reads it from AWS Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store or Vault at plan time. Be aware sensitive only hides values from console output: they are stored in plain text in the state file, which is why state needs encryption and restricted access regardless.
What is the difference between a variable and a local value?

A variable is an input from outside the configuration. Something a caller supplies, and which differs between environments. A local is a value computed inside the configuration from variables, resources or expressions, and it cannot be overridden from outside. The rule of thumb: if someone deploying needs to choose it, make it a variable; if it is derived logic you want to name once and reuse, make it a local.
How do variable validation blocks work?

A validation block inside a variable declaration runs a condition against the supplied value and fails with your error message if it does not hold. This catches bad input at plan time with a clear explanation, rather than producing a confusing provider error later. For example rejecting an environment name that is not one of dev, staging or prod, or an instance type outside an approved list. It is one of the cheapest ways to make a module pleasant for other people to use.
Should every value be a variable?

No. Over-parameterising is a common mistake that makes a module hard to use and hard to reason about, because a caller faces twenty decisions where three would do. Make something a variable when it genuinely differs between callers or environments; use a local for internal logic, and hardcode values that should not vary. A module with sensible defaults and a small required surface is far more usable than one exposing every attribute.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
terraform-input-variables.markdown:
## What Are Terraform Input Variables?

Terraform input variables are named values that let you **parameterize** your infrastructure code. Instead of hardcoding settings like AWS region, instance type, environment name, or subnet CIDR ranges directly into resources, you define variables and then pass values into them when Terraform runs.

Think of a Terraform module like a function in a programming language. A function becomes reusable because it accepts parameters. Terraform modules work the same way. Input variables are the parameters of your infrastructure code.

Without variables, you might write something like this:

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0abcdef1234567890"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  tags = {
    Name        = "dev-web-1"
    Environment = "dev"
  }
}
```

This works, but it is rigid. If you want a staging environment that uses `t3.small`, or a production environment that uses `t3.medium`, you have to edit the file itself. That is fragile and inconvenient.

With variables, the configuration becomes reusable:

```hcl
variable "instance_type" {
  description = "EC2 instance type for the web server"
  type        = string
  default     = "t3.micro"
}

variable "environment" {
  description = "Deployment environment name"
  type        = string
}

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0abcdef1234567890"
  instance_type = var.instance_type

  tags = {
    Name        = "${var.environment}-web-1"
    Environment = var.environment
  }
}
```

Now the same code can be used in development, staging, and production by passing different values.

## Why Use Input Variables?

Terraform input variables solve several real-world problems for DevOps teams:

### 1. Reusability

A single configuration can be reused in different environments. For example:

- `dev` uses smaller instances
- `staging` uses similar settings to production
- `production` uses larger instances and more replicas

### 2. Cleaner code

Hardcoded values scattered across resources are hard to maintain. Variables pull those decisions into one obvious place.

### 3. Safer collaboration

Instead of editing `.tf` files every time a value changes, teams can provide values using `.tfvars` files, environment variables, or CI/CD pipeline secrets.

### 4. Better module design

If you create modules later, variables become the public interface of the module. A good module clearly defines what callers can customize.

### 5. Validation and documentation

Variables let you describe expected inputs, enforce types, and reject invalid values before Terraform touches real infrastructure.

## Declaring Variables with `variable` Blocks

A Terraform input variable is declared with a `variable` block:

```hcl
variable "region" {
  description = "AWS region to deploy into"
  type        = string
  default     = "us-east-1"
}
```

The label after `variable` is the variable name. You reference it elsewhere using `var.<name>`.

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = var.region
}
```

### Common arguments in a variable block

| Argument | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `description` | Explains what the variable is for |
| `type` | Restricts the kind of value Terraform accepts |
| `default` | Makes the variable optional by providing a fallback value |
| `sensitive` | Hides the value in CLI output |
| `validation` | Adds custom rules beyond the basic type check |


A well-defined variable block usually contains at least `description` and `type`, and often `default` if the value should be optional.

## Required Variables vs Optional Variables

A variable is **required** when it has **no `default`** value.

```hcl
variable "project_name" {
  description = "Project identifier used in resource names"
  type        = string
}
```

If you run Terraform without providing a value, Terraform will stop and ask for one, or fail in automation.

A variable is **optional** when it has a `default`.

```hcl
variable "enable_monitoring" {
  description = "Enable CloudWatch detailed monitoring"
  type        = bool
  default     = false
}
```

If the caller does not supply a value, Terraform uses `false`.

### Practical rule

- Use **required variables** for values that must be explicitly chosen, such as environment name, VPC CIDR, or database password.
- Use **optional variables** for safe defaults, such as tags, monitoring toggles, or standard instance types for learning environments.

## Terraform Variable Types

Terraform supports rich type constraints. Defining types is important because it catches mistakes early and makes your configuration self-documenting.

## `string`

A `string` is plain text.

```hcl
variable "environment" {
  description = "Environment name such as dev, staging, or prod"
  type        = string
}
```

Example use:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "${var.environment}-application-logs"
}
```

Typical string values include:

- region names
- environment names
- project names
- AMI IDs
- DNS names

## `number`

A `number` is used for integer or decimal values.

```hcl
variable "instance_count" {
  description = "Number of EC2 instances to create"
  type        = number
  default     = 2
}
```

Example use:

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  count         = var.instance_count
  ami           = "ami-0abcdef1234567890"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
}
```

Common number values include:

- replica counts
- disk sizes
- port numbers
- retention days

## `bool`

A boolean can only be `true` or `false`.

```hcl
variable "enable_versioning" {
  description = "Enable S3 versioning"
  type        = bool
  default     = true
}
```

Example use:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "example" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.example.id

  versioning_configuration {
    status = var.enable_versioning ? "Enabled" : "Suspended"
  }
}
```

Boolean variables are especially useful for optional features.

## `list`

A list is an ordered collection of values of the same type.

```hcl
variable "availability_zones" {
  description = "AZs used for public subnets"
  type        = list(string)
  default     = ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
}
```

Example use:

```hcl
resource "aws_subnet" "public" {
  count             = length(var.availability_zones)
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  availability_zone = var.availability_zones[count.index]
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(var.vpc_cidr, 8, count.index)
}
```

Lists are common when you need:

- multiple subnet IDs
- multiple CIDR blocks
- allowed IP ranges
- lists of domains

## `map`

A map stores key-value pairs of the same value type.

```hcl
variable "tags" {
  description = "Common tags applied to all resources"
  type        = map(string)
  default = {
    ManagedBy = "Terraform"
    Owner     = "platform-team"
  }
}
```

Example use:

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0abcdef1234567890"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  tags          = var.tags
}
```

Maps are very useful for:

- tags
- environment-specific settings
- lookup values keyed by environment

For example:

```hcl
variable "instance_sizes" {
  type = map(string)
  default = {
    dev     = "t3.micro"
    staging = "t3.small"
    prod    = "t3.medium"
  }
}
```

Then you can do:

```hcl
instance_type = var.instance_sizes[var.environment]
```

## `object`

An object groups multiple named attributes, each with its own type.

```hcl
variable "app_config" {
  description = "Application infrastructure settings"
  type = object({
    instance_type   = string
    instance_count  = number
    enable_https    = bool
    root_disk_size  = number
  })
}
```

Example value:

```hcl
app_config = {
  instance_type  = "t3.small"
  instance_count = 2
  enable_https   = true
  root_disk_size = 30
}
```

Example use:

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  count         = var.app_config.instance_count
  ami           = "ami-0abcdef1234567890"
  instance_type = var.app_config.instance_type
}
```

Objects are excellent when related settings belong together.

## `tuple`

A tuple is an ordered sequence where each position can have a different type.

```hcl
variable "maintenance_window" {
  description = "Day, start hour, and whether the window is enabled"
  type        = tuple([string, number, bool])
  default     = ["Sunday", 2, true]
}
```

Example access:

```hcl
locals {
  maintenance_day     = var.maintenance_window[0]
  maintenance_hour    = var.maintenance_window[1]
  maintenance_enabled = var.maintenance_window[2]
}
```

Tuples are supported, but they are less common in beginner Terraform code. In many cases, an `object` is easier to read because attribute names are clearer than positional indexes.

## A Realistic Variable Set

Here is a more complete example for a small web application:

```hcl
variable "project_name" {
  description = "Project name used for tagging and naming"
  type        = string
}

variable "environment" {
  description = "Deployment environment"
  type        = string
}

variable "region" {
  description = "AWS region"
  type        = string
  default     = "us-east-1"
}

variable "instance_type" {
  description = "EC2 instance type"
  type        = string
  default     = "t3.micro"
}

variable "instance_count" {
  description = "Number of EC2 instances"
  type        = number
  default     = 2
}

variable "subnet_ids" {
  description = "Subnets where the app instances will run"
  type        = list(string)
}

variable "tags" {
  description = "Additional resource tags"
  type        = map(string)
  default     = {}
}
```

This is the kind of interface you will see in well-written Terraform modules.

## Variable Validation Blocks

Type constraints are useful, but sometimes they are not enough. A value can have the right type and still be invalid.

For example:

- a string might need to be one of a few allowed environments
- a number might need to be within a range
- a CIDR block might need a certain format
- a name might need to follow a naming convention

That is where `validation` blocks help.

### Basic validation example

```hcl
variable "environment" {
  description = "Deployment environment"
  type        = string

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be one of: dev, staging, prod."
  }
}
```

If someone sets `environment = "qa"`, Terraform fails before making changes.

### Number range validation

```hcl
variable "root_disk_size" {
  description = "Size of the root volume in GB"
  type        = number
  default     = 20

  validation {
    condition     = var.root_disk_size >= 8 && var.root_disk_size <= 200
    error_message = "root_disk_size must be between 8 and 200 GB."
  }
}
```

### Naming pattern validation

```hcl
variable "project_name" {
  description = "Lowercase project name used in resource names"
  type        = string

  validation {
    condition     = can(regex("^[a-z0-9-]+$", var.project_name))
    error_message = "project_name may contain only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens."
  }
}
```

### Validation for a list

```hcl
variable "allowed_ports" {
  description = "List of inbound ports"
  type        = list(number)
  default     = [80, 443]

  validation {
    condition     = alltrue([for p in var.allowed_ports : p > 0 && p < 65536])
    error_message = "All allowed_ports values must be valid TCP/UDP ports between 1 and 65535."
  }
}
```

Validation is one of the simplest ways to make Terraform safer for teams. It turns vague mistakes into clear, actionable errors.

## Assigning Variable Values

Declaring a variable only defines the interface. You still need a way to provide actual values.

Terraform supports multiple input methods.

## 1. `terraform.tfvars`

If a file named `terraform.tfvars` exists in the root module directory, Terraform automatically loads it.

```hcl
project_name  = "billing-app"
environment   = "dev"
instance_type = "t3.micro"
instance_count = 1
```

This is convenient for local development or small demos.

## 2. `*.auto.tfvars`

Any file ending in `.auto.tfvars` or `.auto.tfvars.json` is also loaded automatically.

Example:

```hcl
# dev.auto.tfvars
project_name  = "billing-app"
environment   = "dev"
instance_type = "t3.micro"
```

```hcl
# prod.auto.tfvars
project_name   = "billing-app"
environment    = "prod"
instance_type  = "t3.medium"
instance_count = 3
```

These files are useful when you want separate environment-specific values.

## 3. `-var` flag

You can pass individual values directly on the command line:

```bash
terraform plan -var="environment=staging" -var="instance_count=2"
```

This is useful for quick experiments, but it becomes hard to manage when many variables are involved.

## 4. `-var-file` flag

You can explicitly tell Terraform which variable file to load:

```bash
terraform plan -var-file="dev.tfvars"
terraform apply -var-file="prod.tfvars"
```

This is a common pattern for different environments:

```bash
terraform plan -var-file="environments/dev.tfvars"
terraform plan -var-file="environments/staging.tfvars"
terraform plan -var-file="environments/prod.tfvars"
```

## 5. Environment variables with `TF_VAR_`

Terraform also reads environment variables prefixed with `TF_VAR_`.

```bash
export TF_VAR_environment="prod"
export TF_VAR_instance_type="t3.medium"
export TF_VAR_db_password="SuperSecretPassword"
terraform apply
```

The variable name after `TF_VAR_` must match the Terraform variable name.

This is especially useful in CI/CD pipelines because secrets can be injected from the platform instead of stored in files.

## Which method should you use?

A practical beginner-friendly pattern is:

- use `default` for safe, common values
- use `*.tfvars` or `-var-file` for environment-specific settings
- use `TF_VAR_` for secrets in CI/CD
- use `-var` only for quick one-off overrides

## Sensitive Variables

Some variables contain secrets such as:

- database passwords
- API tokens
- private keys
- access credentials

Mark them as sensitive:

```hcl
variable "db_password" {
  description = "Database administrator password"
  type        = string
  sensitive   = true
}
```

When Terraform shows a plan or apply output, it hides the value:

```text
password = (sensitive value)
```

That reduces accidental exposure in terminal logs and screenshots.

### Important limitation

`sensitive = true` hides the value in CLI output, but it does **not** remove the value from Terraform state. If a provider stores the secret in state, the state file can still contain it. That is one reason remote state security matters.

## Real Example: Variables for an S3 Logging Bucket

```hcl
variable "bucket_name" {
  description = "Globally unique S3 bucket name"
  type        = string

  validation {
    condition     = length(var.bucket_name) >= 3 && length(var.bucket_name) <= 63
    error_message = "bucket_name must be between 3 and 63 characters."
  }
}

variable "environment" {
  description = "Environment name"
  type        = string

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be dev, staging, or prod."
  }
}

variable "enable_versioning" {
  description = "Whether versioning should be enabled"
  type        = bool
  default     = true
}

variable "extra_tags" {
  description = "Additional tags to merge with defaults"
  type        = map(string)
  default     = {}
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = var.bucket_name

  tags = merge(
    {
      Name        = var.bucket_name
      Environment = var.environment
      ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
    },
    var.extra_tags
  )
}
```

This example shows good Terraform design:

- required inputs for important decisions
- defaults for optional behavior
- validation for safer usage
- a map for flexible tagging

## Common Beginner Mistakes

### Not declaring a type

Terraform can infer types in some cases, but explicit type constraints are clearer and safer.

### Using too many command-line `-var` flags

A few are fine. Many are painful. Prefer variable files for stable configurations.

### Storing secrets in committed `.tfvars` files

Never commit real passwords or tokens to Git. Use secure secret injection in your CI/CD platform or secret manager.

### Making everything optional

If a value must be chosen intentionally, do not give it a default. Let Terraform force the caller to think about it.

### Skipping validation

Validation blocks catch bad inputs early and make module usage much friendlier.

## Best Practices for Terraform Input Variables

1. **Always add descriptions.** Your future self and your teammates will thank you.
2. **Always define types.** This prevents confusing runtime issues.
3. **Use required variables for important decisions.** Do not hide critical settings behind weak defaults.
4. **Prefer objects for grouped settings.** They are often clearer than a long flat list of unrelated variables.
5. **Use validation for business rules.** Types alone do not express everything.
6. **Mark secrets as sensitive.** It will not solve every security concern, but it is still important.
7. **Keep the interface simple.** A module with 40 variables is harder to use than one with 8 well-designed inputs.

## Final Thoughts

Input variables are one of the foundations of real-world Terraform. They make the difference between a one-off script and reusable infrastructure as code. Once you understand variables, you can create modules that work across multiple environments, pass values cleanly from CI/CD systems, validate user input, and keep your Terraform code easier to maintain.

A simple way to remember them is this:

- **Variables accept input**
- **Types protect input**
- **Defaults simplify input**
- **Validation improves input**
- **Sensitive flags hide input in CLI output**

Mastering these basics will make every later Terraform topic, from modules to remote state, much easier.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do variable validation blocks work?**

For example rejecting an environment name that is not one of `dev`, `staging` or `prod`, or an instance type outside an approved list. **Should every value be a variable?**

No. Over-parameterising is a common mistake that makes a module hard to use and hard to reason about, because a caller faces twenty decisions where three would do. sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between locals and variables in Terraform?

A variable is an input supplied from outside, by a tfvars file, the command line, or a calling module, and can differ per environment. A local is computed inside the configuration and cannot be overridden externally. Use a variable when the person deploying needs to choose the value; use a local when you want to name a derived value once and reuse it. Locals are evaluated after variables, so they can reference them.
When should I use a local instead of repeating an expression?

Whenever the same expression appears more than twice, or whenever naming it makes the configuration easier to read. A local such as name_prefix = "${var.project}-${var.environment}" used across twenty resources means one place to change the convention, and the intent is obvious at every use site. The common-tags pattern, a locals block merging standard tags with per-resource ones, is the single most useful application.
Can locals reference other locals?

Yes, as long as there is no circular reference. Terraform resolves them as a dependency graph, so a local can build on another declared above or below it in the file. Locals can also reference variables, data sources and resource attributes. What they cannot do is reference something that depends on them, which produces a cycle error naming the chain.
Are locals evaluated once or per resource?

Once per plan or apply, not per resource that references them. The value is computed and reused, so a local containing an expensive expression is not recalculated for each use. Note that a local referencing a resource attribute that is unknown until apply will itself be unknown at plan time, which is why a plan sometimes shows (known after apply) in a place you expected a concrete value.
Can I use locals to avoid repeating tags?

Yes, and it is the idiomatic pattern. Define a common_tags local containing your organisation's standard tags, then merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "..." }) on each resource to add specifics. Many providers also support default_tags at the provider level, which applies tags to every resource automatically. Combining the two gives you provider-wide defaults plus per-resource additions with no repetition.
Can I overuse locals?

Yes. A configuration where every value is indirected through a local becomes harder to follow than one with a few literals, because reading any resource means jumping to the locals block and back. Reserve them for values used in several places, for expressions complex enough that a name aids comprehension, and for anything you expect to change. A single-use local wrapping a simple literal usually costs more in navigation than it saves.

terraform-local-values.markdown:
## What Are Local Values in Terraform?

Terraform local values, usually just called **locals**, are named expressions defined inside a `locals` block. They let you store a calculated value once and then reuse it throughout your configuration.

If input variables are the values that come **into** your Terraform code, local values are the values you compute and organize **inside** it.

A basic example looks like this:

```hcl
variable "environment" {
  type = string
}

variable "project_name" {
  type = string
}

locals {
  name_prefix = "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "${local.name_prefix}-logs"
}
```

Here, `local.name_prefix` saves you from repeating the same string construction everywhere.

Locals do not accept input from the user. They are not part of the public interface of a module. They are strictly an internal convenience that improves readability and removes duplication.

## Why Local Values Matter

Beginners sometimes skip locals and write everything inline. Terraform allows that, but the configuration becomes noisy very quickly.

For example:

```hcl
resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "app" {
  name = "/aws/${var.project_name}/${var.environment}/app"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}-logs"
}

resource "aws_iam_role" "app" {
  name = "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}-app-role"
}
```

The repeated `project_name + environment` pattern appears everywhere. If your naming convention changes, you have to update many places.

With locals:

```hcl
locals {
  name_prefix = "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}"
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "app" {
  name = "/aws/${local.name_prefix}/app"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "${local.name_prefix}-logs"
}

resource "aws_iam_role" "app" {
  name = "${local.name_prefix}-app-role"
}
```

This is easier to read and easier to change.

## Defining Locals with the `locals` Block

A `locals` block can define one or many local values:

```hcl
locals {
  environment_upper = upper(var.environment)
  common_tags = {
    Environment = var.environment
    Project     = var.project_name
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
  }
  enable_backups = var.environment == "prod"
}
```

You reference them with `local.<name>`:

```hcl
tags = local.common_tags
```

Note the syntax carefully:

- `var.name` for input variables
- `local.name` for local values
- `module.name.output_name` for module outputs

## When to Use Locals vs Variables vs Data Sources

This is one of the most important conceptual distinctions in Terraform.

## Use a variable when the value should come from outside

Variables are for values that should be supplied by:

- the person running Terraform
- a parent module
- a `.tfvars` file
- a CI/CD pipeline

Example:

```hcl
variable "region" {
  type = string
}
```

The region is a decision the caller should make, so it belongs in a variable.

## Use a local when the value is internal logic

Locals are for values derived from variables, resources, or expressions inside the module.

Example:

```hcl
locals {
  bucket_name = "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}-logs"
}
```

This does not need to be exposed to the caller. It is implementation detail.

## Use a data source when Terraform must query an external system

Data sources fetch existing information from a provider.

Example:

```hcl
data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {}
```

This value comes from AWS, not from the user and not from pure local computation.

## Quick decision guide

Ask this question:

- **Should a caller choose this value?** Use a variable.
- **Can Terraform calculate this value from what it already knows?** Use a local.
- **Must Terraform ask a provider for this value?** Use a data source.

Understanding this boundary keeps your module interfaces clean.

## Using Expressions in Locals

Local values can contain almost any Terraform expression. This makes them very powerful.

## String expressions

```hcl
locals {
  name_prefix = "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}"
  log_group   = "/aws/${var.project_name}/${var.environment}/app"
}
```

## Arithmetic expressions

```hcl
locals {
  desired_capacity = var.environment == "prod" ? 4 : 2
  total_disk_size  = var.instance_count * var.disk_size_gb
}
```

## Map and list expressions

```hcl
locals {
  common_tags = {
    Project     = var.project_name
    Environment = var.environment
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
  }

  private_subnet_names = [
    for index, az in var.availability_zones :
    "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}-private-${index + 1}"
  ]
}
```

## Referencing resources

Locals can use resource attributes too:

```hcl
locals {
  alb_dns_name = aws_lb.app.dns_name
}
```

This is valid, but use it thoughtfully. If the value is only used once, creating a local may add unnecessary indirection.

## Using Functions in Locals

Terraform includes many built-in functions, and locals are a great place to use them.

## `merge()`

A classic pattern is combining default tags with user-supplied tags.

```hcl
variable "tags" {
  type    = map(string)
  default = {}
}

locals {
  common_tags = merge(
    {
      Project     = var.project_name
      Environment = var.environment
      ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
    },
    var.tags
  )
}
```

Now every resource can reuse `local.common_tags`.

## `lower()`, `upper()`, `replace()`

Useful for naming standards:

```hcl
locals {
  normalized_project = replace(lower(var.project_name), "_", "-")
  name_prefix        = "${local.normalized_project}-${var.environment}"
}
```

## `concat()` and `distinct()`

Useful for combining lists:

```hcl
locals {
  all_cidrs = distinct(concat(var.office_cidrs, var.vpn_cidrs))
}
```

## `lookup()`

A common way to choose environment-specific values:

```hcl
locals {
  instance_size = lookup(
    {
      dev     = "t3.micro"
      staging = "t3.small"
      prod    = "t3.medium"
    },
    var.environment,
    "t3.micro"
  )
}
```

## `jsonencode()`

Great for IAM policies or ECS task definitions:

```hcl
locals {
  bucket_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [
      {
        Effect   = "Allow"
        Action   = ["s3:GetObject"]
        Resource = "${aws_s3_bucket.assets.arn}/*"
      }
    ]
  })
}
```

This keeps complex JSON generation readable.

## Using Conditionals in Locals

Locals often centralize environment-specific decisions.

```hcl
locals {
  instance_type = var.environment == "prod" ? "t3.medium" : "t3.micro"
  backup_days   = var.environment == "prod" ? 30 : 7
  multi_az      = var.environment == "prod" ? true : false
}
```

Now you express the rule once and reuse it everywhere.

You can also make conditionals more expressive by grouping them in locals rather than scattering ternary operators across resource blocks.

## Common Patterns for Local Values

## 1. Common tags

This is probably the most common real-world use of locals.

```hcl
locals {
  common_tags = merge(
    {
      Project     = var.project_name
      Environment = var.environment
      ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
      Owner       = "platform-team"
    },
    var.extra_tags
  )
}
```

Then:

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0abcdef1234567890"
  instance_type = var.instance_type
  tags          = local.common_tags
}
```

This keeps tags consistent across your infrastructure.

## 2. Name prefixes

```hcl
locals {
  name_prefix = "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}"
}
```

Then:

```hcl
resource "aws_security_group" "app" {
  name = "${local.name_prefix}-sg"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "artifacts" {
  bucket = "${local.name_prefix}-artifacts"
}
```

If the naming convention changes later, you update one local value instead of many resources.

## 3. Environment-specific values

```hcl
locals {
  desired_count = {
    dev     = 1
    staging = 2
    prod    = 4
  }[var.environment]
}
```

This is cleaner than repeating the same environment branching logic in multiple places.

## 4. Standardized subnet names

```hcl
locals {
  public_subnet_names = [
    for index, az in var.availability_zones :
    "${var.project_name}-${var.environment}-public-${index + 1}"
  ]
}
```

## 5. Feature flags derived from environment

```hcl
locals {
  enable_waf        = var.environment == "prod"
  enable_monitoring = contains(["staging", "prod"], var.environment)
}
```

This keeps business rules in one place.

## A Complete Example

```hcl
variable "project_name" {
  type = string
}

variable "environment" {
  type = string
}

variable "availability_zones" {
  type = list(string)
}

variable "extra_tags" {
  type    = map(string)
  default = {}
}

locals {
  normalized_project = replace(lower(var.project_name), "_", "-")
  name_prefix        = "${local.normalized_project}-${var.environment}"

  common_tags = merge(
    {
      Project     = var.project_name
      Environment = var.environment
      ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
    },
    var.extra_tags
  )

  instance_type = {
    dev     = "t3.micro"
    staging = "t3.small"
    prod    = "t3.medium"
  }[var.environment]

  backup_retention_days = var.environment == "prod" ? 30 : 7
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "${local.name_prefix}-logs"
  tags   = local.common_tags
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "app" {
  allocated_storage      = 20
  engine                 = "postgres"
  instance_class         = local.instance_type == "t3.medium" ? "db.t3.medium" : "db.t3.micro"
  backup_retention_period = local.backup_retention_days
}
```

This demonstrates the main purpose of locals: moving repeated logic and naming rules into one understandable section.

## Avoiding Overuse of Locals

Locals are helpful, but too many locals can make Terraform harder to read.

### Bad pattern: creating locals for trivial values

```hcl
locals {
  bucket_acl = "private"
}
```

If a value is only used once and adds no clarity, keeping it inline may be simpler.

### Bad pattern: turning every resource attribute into a local

```hcl
locals {
  s3_bucket_id = aws_s3_bucket.logs.id
}
```

If you use that ID once, just reference `aws_s3_bucket.logs.id` directly.

### Bad pattern: hiding module inputs behind unnecessary locals

```hcl
locals {
  region = var.region
}
```

This adds one more name without adding meaning.

## Good rule of thumb

Use locals when they do at least one of these things:

- remove repetition
- clarify intent
- group related logic
- centralize naming or tagging rules
- simplify complex expressions

If a local does none of those things, it may not be worth creating.

## Best Practices for Terraform Locals

1. **Use clear names.** `name_prefix`, `common_tags`, and `backup_retention_days` are much better than `x` or `config1`.
2. **Group related locals together.** Keep naming, tagging, and environment-specific settings organized.
3. **Prefer locals for internal logic.** Do not expose implementation details as variables unless callers truly need to control them.
4. **Do not over-abstract.** Terraform is configuration, not a general-purpose programming language.
5. **Keep module interfaces small.** Use locals to compute internal values from a smaller set of inputs.

## Final Thoughts

Local values are one of the easiest ways to make Terraform code more readable. They help you avoid copy-paste, keep naming conventions consistent, and express environment-specific logic once instead of in ten different places.

A useful mental model is:

- **Variables** are inputs chosen by the caller
- **Locals** are internal calculations chosen by the module author
- **Data sources** are external facts retrieved from the provider

If you apply that rule consistently, your Terraform code will be easier to understand and easier to maintain as it grows.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between locals and variables in Terraform?**

A variable is an input supplied from outside, by a tfvars file, the command line, or a calling module, and can differ per environment. A local is computed inside the configuration and cannot be overridden externally. Use a variable when the person deploying needs to choose the value; use a local when you want to name a derived value once and reuse it. Locals are evaluated after variables, so they can reference them.

**When should I use a local instead of repeating an expression?**

A local such as `name_prefix = "${var.project}-${var.environment}"` used across twenty resources means one place to change the convention, and the intent is obvious at every use site. The common-tags pattern, a `locals` block merging standard tags with per-resource ones, is the single most useful application.

**Can locals reference other locals?**

Yes, as long as there is no circular reference. Terraform resolves them as a dependency graph, so a local can build on another declared above or below it in the file. Locals can also reference variables, data sources and resource attributes. What they cannot do is reference something that depends on them, which produces a cycle error naming the chain.

**Are locals evaluated once or per resource?**

Once per plan or apply, not per resource that references them. The value is computed and reused, so a local containing an expensive expression is not recalculated for each use. Note that a local referencing a resource attribute that is unknown until apply will itself be unknown at plan time, which is why a plan sometimes shows `(known after apply)` in a place you expected a concrete value.

**Can I use locals to avoid repeating tags?**

Yes, and it is the idiomatic pattern. Define a `common_tags` local containing your organisation's standard tags, then `merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "..." })` on each resource to add specifics. Many providers also support `default_tags` at the provider level, which applies tags to every resource automatically. Combining the two gives you provider-wide defaults plus per-resource additions with no repetition.

**Can I overuse locals?**

Yes. A configuration where every value is indirected through a local becomes harder to follow than one with a few literals, because reading any resource means jumping to the locals block and back. Reserve them for values used in several places, for expressions complex enough that a name aids comprehension, and for anything you expect to change. A single-use local wrapping a simple literal usually costs more in navigation than it saves.

sections.title: What Are Output Values in Terraform?
paragraphs: Terraform output values are named results that Terraform prints after it creates or updates infrastructure. They answer a simple but important question: after Terraform finishes, how do you get back the values you care about?
For example, after creating infrastructure you often want to know:
Those values usually come from resources created during terraform apply. Output values make them easy to expose in a clean, reusable way.
A basic example looks like this:
After terraform apply, Terraform can display the result:
Output values are useful for both humans and automation. A person can quickly see important infrastructure details, while a CI/CD script can read outputs and pass them to later steps.

sections.title: Why Output Values Matter
paragraphs: It is possible to inspect Terraform state manually, but that is not a good workflow. State is verbose, internal, and often sensitive. Output values give you a small curated interface to the most important results.
They help in several ways:
Instead of searching through a long plan or cloud console, you can expose exactly what matters.
Outputs are how child modules publish values back to the root module or to other modules.
Deployment scripts, Ansible playbooks, Kubernetes bootstrap steps, and CI/CD jobs often depend on values generated by Terraform.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What are Terraform outputs used for?

They expose values from a configuration, an IP address, a DNS name, a database endpoint, a generated ARN, so that they can be read after apply, consumed by a calling module, or picked up by a CI script. Within a module, outputs are the only way to return anything to the caller: a parent module cannot reach inside a child to read a resource attribute directly. Outputs are also how humans find the URL of what they just deployed.
How do I read an output value?

terraform output prints them all, terraform output name prints one, and terraform output -json produces machine-readable output for scripts to parse with jq. The -raw flag prints a single string value without quotes, which is what you want when interpolating into a shell command. Outputs are read from state, so they are available any time after apply without re-running anything.
What does marking an output sensitive actually do?

It redacts the value in terraform plan and terraform apply console output, showing (sensitive value) instead. That is all. The value is still stored in plain text in the state file, still returned by terraform output -json, and still visible to anyone who can read state. It protects against a secret appearing in a CI log or a screenshot. It is not encryption, and it is not an access control.
Why does my output show "known after apply" in the plan?

Because it depends on an attribute that does not exist until the resource is created: an auto-generated ID, an assigned IP address, an ARN. Terraform cannot know it at plan time, so it shows a placeholder. This is normal and requires no action. If an output you expected to be static shows this, it is referencing a resource attribute rather than a variable or literal.
How do I pass outputs between modules?

A child module declares an output, and the parent references it as module.<name>.<output>. That value can then be passed as an input to another module, which is how you wire a network module's subnet IDs into a compute module. For passing values between separate root configurations with separate state, use a terraform_remote_state data source, though many teams prefer writing the value to SSM Parameter Store and reading it back, which avoids coupling one configuration's state to another's.
Can I use outputs in CI/CD pipelines?

Yes, and it is the standard way to hand values to later steps. Run terraform output -json > outputs.json and parse it, or use -raw to capture a single value into a shell variable. Typical uses are passing a load balancer DNS name to a smoke test, an ECR repository URL to a build step, or a cluster name to a deployment job. Remember sensitive outputs appear unredacted in -json, so avoid printing the whole document into a log.
