sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Configure the Terraform AWS provider, authenticate without long-lived keys using assume role and OIDC, manage regions and accounts, and tag everything.

The AWS provider is the most used Terraform provider by a wide margin. The mechanics of writing resources are covered in the pages below. This page is about the decisions that surround them: how Terraform authenticates, how you handle more than one region or account, and the conventions that stop an estate becoming unmanageable.

sections.title: Provider configuration
paragraphs: Two things worth doing from the start.

Pin the provider version with a pessimistic constraint. AWS provider major versions carry breaking changes. The v4 release split aws_s3_bucket inline blocks into separate resources, which broke a great many configurations that had not pinned.

Use default_tags. Every resource that supports tagging gets these automatically, with no repetition. It is the cheapest way to make cost allocation and ownership work, and retrofitting tags across an existing estate is tedious.

sections.title: Authentication
paragraphs: Terraform uses the standard AWS credential chain, so it picks up whatever the AWS CLI would. In order of preference:
OIDC federation in CI: the right answer for pipelines. No stored credentials at all:
The pipeline exchanges a signed token for temporary credentials, and the role's trust policy restricts which repository and branch may do so. Nothing long-lived exists to leak or rotate.
A named profile locally:
Assume-role in the provider block, which is how one configuration manages several accounts.
What not to do: hardcode access_key and secret_key in the provider block. They end up in version control, and they are unnecessary in every environment where Terraform actually runs.
Always confirm which identity you are using before applying:
Pointing at the wrong account is the most expensive Terraform mistake available, and nothing in the plan output warns you.

sections.title: Multiple regions and accounts
paragraphs: A provider block covers one region and one account. For more, use aliases:
That ACM example is the one almost everyone meets. CloudFront only accepts certificates from us-east-1 regardless of where the rest of the stack lives.
For modules that need a non-default provider, pass it explicitly:
Modules must never declare their own provider block. They declare required_providers and inherit configuration from the root.

sections.title: Structuring an AWS estate
paragraphs: The pattern that scales:

Each environment is a root module calling shared modules with different values. State is separate per environment, so a staging mistake cannot touch production state, and credentials can be scoped so a staging pipeline cannot reach production at all.

Split by change frequency, not just by environment. Networking changes rarely and is shared; application infrastructure changes constantly. Keeping them in one state means every deploy plans against the whole VPC and a mistake has a wider blast radius. Put the VPC in its own configuration and expose IDs as outputs.

codeBlock.code:
environments/
├── production/     # own backend key, own state, own credentials
├── staging/
└── dev/
modules/
├── network/
├── application/
└── data/

sections.title: Reading values from elsewhere
paragraphs: To consume another configuration's output, terraform_remote_state works but couples the two tightly and requires read access to state, which contains secrets.
A looser alternative is publishing to SSM Parameter Store and reading it back:
Also stop hardcoding AMI IDs. AWS publishes current images as public SSM parameters:

sections.title: Things that bite
paragraphs: Resource replacement on immutable attributes. Subnet CIDRs, availability zones, RDS engine versions in some cases. The plan shows -/+ with a # forces replacement annotation. Read every plan for that marker before applying to anything stateful.
Eventual consistency. IAM in particular propagates slowly, so a role created and used in the same apply occasionally fails. Explicit depends_on helps; a retry sometimes is the pragmatic answer.
Provider v4 S3 changes. Versioning, encryption and public access blocks are now separate resources rather than inline blocks. Older tutorials will not work.
Service quotas. Terraform surfaces the API error, which often reads as a permissions problem. Check quotas before assuming IAM.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: The Terraform part of AWS work is rarely the hard part. What determines whether an estate stays manageable is the surrounding decisions: pin the provider, tag by default, authenticate with roles rather than keys, keep state separate per environment, and split configurations by how often they change. Get those right early and the resource blocks look after themselves.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How should Terraform authenticate to AWS?

Through the standard credential chain, never with keys hardcoded in the provider block. Locally, use a named profile via AWS_PROFILE or AWS SSO. In CI, use OIDC federation. The pipeline exchanges a short-lived signed token for temporary credentials through an IAM role whose trust policy restricts which repository and branch may assume it. That removes long-lived credentials entirely, so there is nothing to rotate and nothing useful in a leaked log.
How do I use Terraform across multiple AWS regions?

Declare additional provider blocks with an alias, then set provider = aws.us_east_1 on resources that belong in the other region. The case everyone meets is ACM certificates for CloudFront, which must be issued in us-east-1 regardless of where the rest of the infrastructure lives. To use an aliased provider inside a module, pass it explicitly through the providers argument. Modules should never declare their own provider configuration.
How do I manage multiple AWS accounts with Terraform?

Use assume_role in the provider block, pointing at a role in the target account, with aliases when one configuration spans several accounts. More commonly, keep each account's infrastructure in its own root configuration with its own backend and credentials, which gives genuine isolation. A pipeline for staging then physically cannot reach production. AWS Organizations plus IAM Identity Center makes the role structure straightforward.
Why does Terraform want to replace my AWS resource instead of updating it?

Because you changed an attribute AWS cannot modify in place: a subnet's CIDR block, an instance's availability zone, certain database engine settings. The plan marks it -/+ and annotates the specific attribute with # forces replacement, so the cause is always stated. On stateless resources this is harmless; on anything storing data it is destructive. Protect critical resources with lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } so a replacement cannot be applied accidentally.
How do I tag all my AWS resources consistently?

Use default_tags in the provider block, which applies the tags to every resource that supports tagging, with no repetition. Add per-resource tags normally and they merge with the defaults. This is the cheapest way to make cost allocation, ownership and automated cleanup work, and it is considerably easier to set up at the start than to retrofit across an existing estate.
Should the VPC and the application be in the same Terraform configuration?

Usually not. Networking changes rarely and is shared by many workloads; application infrastructure changes constantly. Combining them means every application deploy plans against the whole network, the blast radius of a mistake is larger, and applies are slower. Put the VPC in its own configuration, expose IDs as outputs, and consume them from application configurations through a data source or a value published to SSM Parameter Store.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
terraform-with-aws.markdown:
The AWS provider is the most used Terraform provider by a wide margin. The mechanics of writing resources are covered in the pages below. This page is about the decisions that surround them: how Terraform authenticates, how you handle more than one region or account, and the conventions that stop an estate becoming unmanageable.

## Provider configuration

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.9"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.region

  default_tags {
    tags = {
      Project     = var.project
      Environment = var.environment
      ManagedBy   = "terraform"
    }
  }
}
```

Two things worth doing from the start.

**Pin the provider version** with a pessimistic constraint. AWS provider major versions carry breaking changes. The v4 release split `aws_s3_bucket` inline blocks into separate resources, which broke a great many configurations that had not pinned.

**Use `default_tags`.** Every resource that supports tagging gets these automatically, with no repetition. It is the cheapest way to make cost allocation and ownership work, and retrofitting tags across an existing estate is tedious.

## Authentication

Terraform uses the standard AWS credential chain, so it picks up whatever the AWS CLI would. In order of preference:

**OIDC federation in CI**: the right answer for pipelines. No stored credentials at all:

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
  assume_role {
    role_arn     = "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/TerraformDeploy"
    session_name = "terraform-ci"
  }
}
```

The pipeline exchanges a signed token for temporary credentials, and the role's trust policy restricts which repository and branch may do so. Nothing long-lived exists to leak or rotate.

**A named profile locally**:

```bash
export AWS_PROFILE=acme-staging
terraform plan
```

**Assume-role in the provider block**, which is how one configuration manages several accounts.

What not to do: hardcode `access_key` and `secret_key` in the provider block. They end up in version control, and they are unnecessary in every environment where Terraform actually runs.

Always confirm which identity you are using before applying:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity
```

Pointing at the wrong account is the most expensive Terraform mistake available, and nothing in the plan output warns you.

## Multiple regions and accounts

A provider block covers one region and one account. For more, use **aliases**:

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "us_east_1"
  region = "us-east-1"
}

# CloudFront certificates must live in us-east-1
resource "aws_acm_certificate" "cdn" {
  provider          = aws.us_east_1
  domain_name       = var.domain
  validation_method = "DNS"
}
```

That ACM example is the one almost everyone meets. CloudFront only accepts certificates from `us-east-1` regardless of where the rest of the stack lives.

For modules that need a non-default provider, pass it explicitly:

```hcl
module "cdn" {
  source    = "./modules/cdn"
  providers = { aws = aws.us_east_1 }
}
```

Modules must never declare their own `provider` block. They declare `required_providers` and inherit configuration from the root.

## Structuring an AWS estate

The pattern that scales:

```
environments/
âââ production/     # own backend key, own state, own credentials
âââ staging/
âââ dev/
modules/
âââ network/
âââ application/
âââ data/
```

Each environment is a root module calling shared modules with different values. State is separate per environment, so a staging mistake cannot touch production state, and credentials can be scoped so a staging pipeline cannot reach production at all.

**Split by change frequency, not just by environment.** Networking changes rarely and is shared; application infrastructure changes constantly. Keeping them in one state means every deploy plans against the whole VPC and a mistake has a wider blast radius. Put the VPC in its own configuration and expose IDs as outputs.

## Reading values from elsewhere

To consume another configuration's output, `terraform_remote_state` works but couples the two tightly and requires read access to state, which contains secrets.

A looser alternative is publishing to SSM Parameter Store and reading it back:

```hcl
data "aws_ssm_parameter" "vpc_id" {
  name = "/platform/network/vpc-id"
}
```

Also stop hardcoding AMI IDs. AWS publishes current images as public SSM parameters:

```hcl
data "aws_ssm_parameter" "al2023" {
  name = "/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64"
}
```

## Things that bite

**Resource replacement on immutable attributes.** Subnet CIDRs, availability zones, RDS engine versions in some cases. The plan shows `-/+` with a `# forces replacement` annotation. Read every plan for that marker before applying to anything stateful.

**Eventual consistency.** IAM in particular propagates slowly, so a role created and used in the same apply occasionally fails. Explicit `depends_on` helps; a retry sometimes is the pragmatic answer.

**Provider v4 S3 changes.** Versioning, encryption and public access blocks are now separate resources rather than inline blocks. Older tutorials will not work.

**Service quotas.** Terraform surfaces the API error, which often reads as a permissions problem. Check quotas before assuming IAM.

## Explore further in this section

| Sub-topic | What you will learn |
|---|---|
| [Terraform AWS VPC](/tutorials/terraform/terraform-aws-vpc) | Networking, subnets across AZs, NAT and tagging |
| [Terraform AWS EC2](/tutorials/terraform/terraform-aws-ec2) | Instances, AMIs, launch templates and volumes |
| [Terraform AWS S3](/tutorials/terraform/terraform-aws-s3) | Buckets, the split resources, lifecycle and access |

## Quick reference

| Task | Syntax |
|---|---|
| Pin the provider | `version = "~> 5.0"` in `required_providers` |
| Tag everything | `default_tags { tags = { ... } }` |
| Assume a role | `assume_role { role_arn = "..." }` |
| Second region | `provider "aws" { alias = "us_east_1" ... }` |
| Use an alias | `provider = aws.us_east_1` |
| Pass to a module | `providers = { aws = aws.us_east_1 }` |
| Current AMI | `data "aws_ssm_parameter"` on `/aws/service/ami-...` |
| Check identity | `aws sts get-caller-identity` |
| Available AZs | `data "aws_availability_zones"` |

---

## Final Thoughts

The Terraform part of AWS work is rarely the hard part. What determines whether an estate stays manageable is the surrounding decisions: pin the provider, tag by default, authenticate with roles rather than keys, keep state separate per environment, and split configurations by how often they change. Get those right early and the resource blocks look after themselves.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How should Terraform authenticate to AWS?**

Through the standard credential chain, never with keys hardcoded in the provider block. Locally, use a named profile via `AWS_PROFILE` or AWS SSO. In CI, use OIDC federation. The pipeline exchanges a short-lived signed token for temporary credentials through an IAM role whose trust policy restricts which repository and branch may assume it. That removes long-lived credentials entirely, so there is nothing to rotate and nothing useful in a leaked log.

**How do I use Terraform across multiple AWS regions?**

Declare additional `provider` blocks with an `alias`, then set `provider = aws.us_east_1` on resources that belong in the other region. The case everyone meets is ACM certificates for CloudFront, which must be issued in `us-east-1` regardless of where the rest of the infrastructure lives. To use an aliased provider inside a module, pass it explicitly through the `providers` argument. Modules should never declare their own provider configuration.

**How do I manage multiple AWS accounts with Terraform?**

Use `assume_role` in the provider block, pointing at a role in the target account, with aliases when one configuration spans several accounts. More commonly, keep each account's infrastructure in its own root configuration with its own backend and credentials, which gives genuine isolation. A pipeline for staging then physically cannot reach production. AWS Organizations plus IAM Identity Center makes the role structure straightforward.

**Why does Terraform want to replace my AWS resource instead of updating it?**

Because you changed an attribute AWS cannot modify in place: a subnet's CIDR block, an instance's availability zone, certain database engine settings. The plan marks it `-/+` and annotates the specific attribute with `# forces replacement`, so the cause is always stated. On stateless resources this is harmless; on anything storing data it is destructive. Protect critical resources with `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` so a replacement cannot be applied accidentally.

**How do I tag all my AWS resources consistently?**

Use `default_tags` in the provider block, which applies the tags to every resource that supports tagging, with no repetition. Add per-resource tags normally and they merge with the defaults. This is the cheapest way to make cost allocation, ownership and automated cleanup work, and it is considerably easier to set up at the start than to retrofit across an existing estate.

**Should the VPC and the application be in the same Terraform configuration?**

Usually not. Networking changes rarely and is shared by many workloads; application infrastructure changes constantly. Combining them means every application deploy plans against the whole network, the blast radius of a mistake is larger, and applies are slower. Put the VPC in its own configuration, expose IDs as outputs, and consume them from application configurations through a data source or a value published to SSM Parameter Store.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I write my own VPC module or use the community one?

Use the community terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws module for anything real. VPC networking has a large number of interdependent pieces. Subnets across availability zones, route tables and associations, internet and NAT gateways, endpoints, flow logs, and the module handles combinations that take a long time to get right by hand. Writing your own is a genuinely useful learning exercise, and rarely the best production choice.
How do I create subnets across multiple availability zones?

Query the available zones with the aws_availability_zones data source rather than hardcoding names, then create subnets with for_each over a map keyed on a stable name. Use cidrsubnet() to carve the ranges from the VPC CIDR so they are derived rather than hand-calculated. Avoid count with an index into the AZ list, if AWS changes zone ordering or you remove one, positional identity causes unrelated subnets to be recreated.
How many NAT gateways should Terraform create?

One per availability zone for production, since a NAT gateway is zonal and losing its AZ takes outbound access with it. The community module exposes single_nat_gateway and one_nat_gateway_per_az to control this, and using a single gateway in non-production is a reasonable saving. Be aware NAT gateways are frequently the largest networking cost on an AWS bill, so add free S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints in the same configuration.
Why does changing a subnet CIDR want to destroy and recreate it?

Because a subnet's CIDR block is immutable. AWS provides no way to change it in place, so Terraform must replace the resource. The plan shows -/+ with a "forces replacement" annotation. Anything inside that subnet is affected, so treat CIDR changes as a migration rather than an edit. This is why sizing the VPC and its subnets generously at creation matters: a /20 per subnet costs nothing extra and avoids the problem entirely.
How do I tag subnets for EKS or load balancers?

The AWS Load Balancer Controller and EKS discover where to place resources from subnet tags, kubernetes.io/role/elb set to 1 on public subnets and kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb on private ones, plus a cluster ownership tag. The community VPC module accepts public_subnet_tags and private_subnet_tags for exactly this. Missing tags produce an Ingress that sits in pending with no clear error, which is a slow thing to diagnose.
Should the VPC live in the same Terraform state as my application?

Usually not. Networking changes rarely and is shared by many workloads, while application infrastructure changes constantly. Keeping them together means every application deploy plans against the whole VPC and a mistake has a larger blast radius. Put the VPC in its own configuration and expose IDs via outputs, then consume them from application configurations with a data source or by reading a parameter from SSM.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
terraform-aws-vpc.markdown:
## Project Overview

In this lesson, you are building the network foundation for the rest of the AWS project. The goal is a **custom VPC with both public and private subnets**. Later lessons will place an EC2 web server in a public subnet and store static assets in S3, but neither of those pieces should come first. Good cloud design starts with the network.

The VPC will include:

- one custom `aws_vpc`
- two public subnets
- two private subnets
- an internet gateway for public internet access
- a public route table
- a private route table
- one NAT gateway so private subnets can reach the internet for updates without becoming publicly reachable

That architecture is common because it separates resources by exposure level. Public subnets are for components that must accept traffic from the internet, such as a bastion host, load balancer, or simple demo web server. Private subnets are for application servers, databases, or internal services that should not receive direct inbound traffic from the public internet.

Even if your first Terraform project is small, learning this pattern now pays off later. Most real AWS environments reuse the same ideas repeatedly.

## What We Are Building

Conceptually, the layout looks like this:

```text
VPC 10.0.0.0/16
âââ Public subnet A   10.0.1.0/24
âââ Public subnet B   10.0.2.0/24
âââ Private subnet A  10.0.11.0/24
âââ Private subnet B  10.0.12.0/24
âââ Internet Gateway
âââ NAT Gateway (in a public subnet)
âââ Public route table   -> 0.0.0.0/0 via Internet Gateway
âââ Private route table  -> 0.0.0.0/0 via NAT Gateway
```

A few design principles are worth understanding before you write any code:

### Why public and private subnets?

A subnet becomes âpublicâ when its route table sends outbound internet traffic to an **Internet Gateway** and resources inside it can receive public IP addresses. A subnet stays âprivateâ when it does not expose that direct path.

### Why a NAT gateway?

Private resources often still need outbound internet access. For example:

- an EC2 instance in a private subnet may need to download package updates
- an internal application server may need to call external APIs
- a deployment process may need to fetch software packages

A NAT gateway gives those private resources outbound internet connectivity **without** opening inbound access from the internet.

### Why more than one availability zone?

You will spread subnets across multiple AZs by using the AWS availability zone data source. This is good practice because it prepares the environment for high availability. Even if you launch only one EC2 instance today, you are learning a production-friendly network layout.

## Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have:

1. **An AWS account** with permission to create VPC resources, subnets, route tables, internet gateways, elastic IPs, and NAT gateways.
2. **Terraform installed** and available in your terminal.
3. **AWS credentials configured** locally.
4. A basic understanding of Terraform commands such as `terraform init`, `terraform plan`, and `terraform apply`.

You can provide AWS credentials in several ways:

- environment variables like `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
- an AWS CLI profile in `~/.aws/credentials`
- federated credentials such as AWS SSO

A good quick validation is:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity
terraform version
```

If both commands work, you are ready to continue.

## Project Structure

A simple structure for this lesson looks like this:

```text
terraform-aws-vpc/
âââ main.tf
âââ variables.tf
âââ outputs.tf
âââ terraform.tfvars
```

You can keep everything in a single `main.tf` for practice, but splitting files by purpose makes the configuration easier to read.

## Provider Configuration

Start by telling Terraform which provider you need and which region to target.

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6.0"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}
```

The `required_providers` block locks in the AWS provider source and version constraint. That matters because provider schemas evolve over time. Pinning a version range reduces unpleasant surprises when teammates or CI pipelines run the same configuration.

The provider block uses a variable for region instead of hardcoding it. That makes the project reusable.

In `variables.tf`, define the region and network inputs:

```hcl
variable "aws_region" {
  description = "AWS region for the infrastructure"
  type        = string
  default     = "us-east-1"
}

variable "project_name" {
  description = "Name used in resource tags"
  type        = string
  default     = "devopslesson"
}

variable "vpc_cidr" {
  description = "CIDR block for the VPC"
  type        = string
  default     = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

variable "public_subnet_cidrs" {
  description = "CIDR blocks for public subnets"
  type        = list(string)
  default     = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]
}

variable "private_subnet_cidrs" {
  description = "CIDR blocks for private subnets"
  type        = list(string)
  default     = ["10.0.11.0/24", "10.0.12.0/24"]
}
```

## Discovering Availability Zones with a Data Source

Instead of hardcoding availability zone names, ask AWS for them.

```hcl
data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {
  state = "available"
}
```

Data sources do not create infrastructure. They read information from the provider so you can use that information elsewhere.

Why is this helpful?

- it makes the configuration more portable
- it avoids mistakes from typing the wrong AZ name
- it lets Terraform choose the first two available zones dynamically

You can then refer to:

```hcl
data.aws_availability_zones.available.names[0]
data.aws_availability_zones.available.names[1]
```

## Creating the VPC

Now create the VPC itself.

```hcl
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = var.vpc_cidr
  enable_dns_support   = true
  enable_dns_hostnames = true

  tags = {
    Name        = "${var.project_name}-vpc"
    Environment = "lab"
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
  }
}
```

The key attributes here are:

- `cidr_block`, the IP range for the whole VPC
- `enable_dns_support`, enables DNS resolution inside the VPC
- `enable_dns_hostnames`, lets instances receive DNS hostnames

`enable_dns_hostnames` is especially useful for EC2 and load balancer scenarios. If you skip it, later services may behave in ways that confuse beginners.

### Why use a `/16` CIDR block?

`10.0.0.0/16` gives you a large private IP range to divide into many subnets later. It is a common lab and production starting point because it is roomy without being hard to reason about.

## Creating Public Subnets

Next, create the public subnets.

```hcl
resource "aws_subnet" "public" {
  count = length(var.public_subnet_cidrs)

  vpc_id                  = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block              = var.public_subnet_cidrs[count.index]
  availability_zone       = data.aws_availability_zones.available.names[count.index]
  map_public_ip_on_launch = true

  tags = {
    Name        = "${var.project_name}-public-${count.index + 1}"
    Tier        = "public"
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
  }
}
```

Several ideas come together in this resource:

### `count`

`count` lets one resource block create multiple resources. Because `public_subnet_cidrs` contains two CIDR blocks, Terraform creates two public subnets.

### `availability_zone`

Each subnet gets an availability zone from the data source. Subnet 0 lands in AZ 0, subnet 1 lands in AZ 1.

### `map_public_ip_on_launch = true`

This setting is one of the clearest indicators that these are intended to be public subnets. When an instance launches in one of these subnets, AWS can automatically assign it a public IP address.

That does **not** by itself make the subnet public. You also need a route to an Internet Gateway, which you will create later.

## Creating Private Subnets

Private subnets are almost the same, but one important setting changes.

```hcl
resource "aws_subnet" "private" {
  count = length(var.private_subnet_cidrs)

  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block        = var.private_subnet_cidrs[count.index]
  availability_zone = data.aws_availability_zones.available.names[count.index]

  tags = {
    Name        = "${var.project_name}-private-${count.index + 1}"
    Tier        = "private"
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
  }
}
```

Notice that there is **no** `map_public_ip_on_launch = true` here. Private subnets should not automatically hand public IPs to launched instances.

These private subnets will later use the NAT gateway for outbound access.

## Creating the Internet Gateway

Public internet access for the VPC starts with an internet gateway.

```hcl
resource "aws_internet_gateway" "main" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id

  tags = {
    Name      = "${var.project_name}-igw"
    ManagedBy = "Terraform"
  }
}
```

An Internet Gateway is attached to the VPC, not to an individual subnet. Subnets become internet-routable only when their route table sends traffic to it.

## Creating the Public Route Table

Now define a route table for the public subnets.

```hcl
resource "aws_route_table" "public" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id

  route {
    cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
    gateway_id = aws_internet_gateway.main.id
  }

  tags = {
    Name      = "${var.project_name}-public-rt"
    ManagedBy = "Terraform"
  }
}
```

The route block is the important part:

- destination `0.0.0.0/0` means âall IPv4 addresses not otherwise matchedâ
- `gateway_id = aws_internet_gateway.main.id` says âsend that traffic to the internet gatewayâ

This is what gives public subnets their outbound internet path.

## Associating Public Subnets with the Public Route Table

A route table exists, but it does nothing until subnets use it.

```hcl
resource "aws_route_table_association" "public" {
  count = length(aws_subnet.public)

  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.public[count.index].id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.public.id
}
```

This association explicitly links each public subnet to the public route table.

## Creating the NAT Gateway

Private subnets should not route directly to the Internet Gateway, but they still need outbound connectivity for updates and package downloads. The standard AWS answer is a NAT gateway.

A NAT gateway needs an **Elastic IP** and must be placed in a **public subnet**.

```hcl
resource "aws_eip" "nat" {
  domain = "vpc"

  tags = {
    Name      = "${var.project_name}-nat-eip"
    ManagedBy = "Terraform"
  }
}

resource "aws_nat_gateway" "main" {
  allocation_id = aws_eip.nat.id
  subnet_id     = aws_subnet.public[0].id

  depends_on = [aws_internet_gateway.main]

  tags = {
    Name      = "${var.project_name}-nat"
    ManagedBy = "Terraform"
  }
}
```

### Why is the NAT gateway in a public subnet?

Because it needs public internet reachability itself. Private instances send outbound traffic to the NAT gateway, and the NAT gateway forwards that traffic to the internet on their behalf.

### Why only one NAT gateway in this lesson?

Cost and simplicity. A highly available production design often uses one NAT gateway per AZ, but for a learning project that gets expensive quickly. One NAT gateway is enough to understand the pattern.

## Creating the Private Route Table

Now define the route table for private subnets.

```hcl
resource "aws_route_table" "private" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id

  route {
    cidr_block     = "0.0.0.0/0"
    nat_gateway_id = aws_nat_gateway.main.id
  }

  tags = {
    Name      = "${var.project_name}-private-rt"
    ManagedBy = "Terraform"
  }
}
```

The destination is again `0.0.0.0/0`, but this time the next hop is the NAT gateway instead of the Internet Gateway.

That difference is the essence of private subnet design.

## Associating Private Subnets with the Private Route Table

```hcl
resource "aws_route_table_association" "private" {
  count = length(aws_subnet.private)

  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.private[count.index].id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.private.id
}
```

At this point, the network layout is complete:

- public subnets route to the Internet Gateway
- private subnets route to the NAT gateway

## Running `terraform plan`

Once the configuration exists, initialize the working directory:

```bash
terraform init
```

Then run:

```bash
terraform plan
```

`terraform plan` is not just a formality. It is the review step where Terraform tells you exactly what it intends to create.

For this lesson, expect the plan to show resources similar to:

- 1 VPC
- 2 public subnets
- 2 private subnets
- 1 internet gateway
- 1 elastic IP
- 1 NAT gateway
- 2 route tables
- 4 route table associations
- 1 data source read for availability zones

### What to review in the plan output

Before you apply, scan for these details:

1. **CIDR blocks**: make sure the VPC and subnet ranges are what you intended.
2. **Region and AZs**: confirm Terraform is targeting the correct AWS region.
3. **Public subnet behavior**: verify `map_public_ip_on_launch = true` is present only on the public subnets.
4. **Routing targets**: verify the public route uses the Internet Gateway and the private route uses the NAT gateway.
5. **Tags**: good tags help later when you inspect the AWS console.

The habit to build now is: **never apply infrastructure you have not reviewed**.

## Applying and Verifying the Network

When the plan looks correct, run:

```bash
terraform apply
```

After the apply finishes, verify in the AWS console that:

- the VPC exists with the expected CIDR block
- both public and private subnets were created
- public route table associations point to the Internet Gateway
- private route table associations point to the NAT gateway
- the NAT gateway sits in one of the public subnets

You can also inspect outputs locally:

```bash
terraform output
```

These outputs become useful in the next lesson when the EC2 instance needs to know where to launch.

## Final Thoughts

This lesson teaches one of the most reusable AWS infrastructure patterns you can learn. The exact CIDR ranges, AZ count, and route design may change in larger environments, but the core ideas remain the same:

- define a VPC clearly
- separate public and private network tiers
- route internet-bound traffic intentionally
- review `terraform plan` before every change

With the network in place, you are ready to move on to the compute layer.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Should I write my own VPC module or use the community one?**

Use the community `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` module for anything real. VPC networking has a large number of interdependent pieces. Subnets across availability zones, route tables and associations, internet and NAT gateways, endpoints, flow logs, and the module handles combinations that take a long time to get right by hand. Writing your own is a genuinely useful learning exercise, and rarely the best production choice.

**How do I create subnets across multiple availability zones?**

Query the available zones with the `aws_availability_zones` data source rather than hardcoding names, then create subnets with `for_each` over a map keyed on a stable name. Use `cidrsubnet()` to carve the ranges from the VPC CIDR so they are derived rather than hand-calculated. Avoid `count` with an index into the AZ list, if AWS changes zone ordering or you remove one, positional identity causes unrelated subnets to be recreated.

**How many NAT gateways should Terraform create?**

One per availability zone for production, since a NAT gateway is zonal and losing its AZ takes outbound access with it. The community module exposes `single_nat_gateway` and `one_nat_gateway_per_az` to control this, and using a single gateway in non-production is a reasonable saving. Be aware NAT gateways are frequently the largest networking cost on an AWS bill, so add free S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints in the same configuration.

**Why does changing a subnet CIDR want to destroy and recreate it?**

Because a subnet's CIDR block is immutable. AWS provides no way to change it in place, so Terraform must replace the resource. The plan shows `-/+` with a "forces replacement" annotation. Anything inside that subnet is affected, so treat CIDR changes as a migration rather than an edit. This is why sizing the VPC and its subnets generously at creation matters: a `/20` per subnet costs nothing extra and avoids the problem entirely.

**How do I tag subnets for EKS or load balancers?**

The AWS Load Balancer Controller and EKS discover where to place resources from subnet tags, `kubernetes.io/role/elb` set to `1` on public subnets and `kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb` on private ones, plus a cluster ownership tag. The community VPC module accepts `public_subnet_tags` and `private_subnet_tags` for exactly this. Missing tags produce an Ingress that sits in `pending` with no clear error, which is a slow thing to diagnose.

**Should the VPC live in the same Terraform state as my application?**

Usually not. Networking changes rarely and is shared by many workloads, while application infrastructure changes constantly. Keeping them together means every application deploy plans against the whole VPC and a mistake has a larger blast radius. Put the VPC in its own configuration and expose IDs via outputs, then consume them from application configurations with a data source or by reading a parameter from SSM.

sections.title: Practice Questions
paragraphs: Why is a Terraform `aws_ami` data source usually better than hardcoding an AMI ID?
What is the main benefit of using `user_data` in this EC2 tutorial?
Why attach an Elastic IP to the EC2 instance in this project?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I avoid hardcoding an AMI ID in Terraform?

Use the aws_ami data source with owner and name filters plus most_recent = true, or read AWS's published SSM public parameters with the aws_ssm_parameter data source, /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 resolves the current Amazon Linux image. Both remove a value that goes stale and becomes a security liability. Note that a new AMI then triggers instance replacement, so pair this with a launch template and an Auto Scaling group if you want control over when that happens.
Should I create EC2 instances directly or use a launch template?

Use a launch template with an Auto Scaling group for anything that matters, even at a desired capacity of one. A bare aws_instance is a pet: if it fails, nothing replaces it, and every change risks manual repair. A launch template plus an Auto Scaling group makes replacement routine and gives you rolling updates via instance refresh. Reserve standalone instances for genuinely one-off or experimental work.
How do I pass startup configuration to an instance?

Through user_data, rendered with the templatefile() function so values can be interpolated from Terraform. Use user_data_replace_on_change = true if you want a change to the script to replace the instance, since by default a modified user_data does not affect a running instance. It only executes on first boot. For anything substantial, bake the configuration into an AMI with Packer instead, which makes instances start ready and shortens boot time.
Why does Terraform want to replace my instance when I only changed a tag?

It usually does not, and a replacement means something else changed. Most often the AMI ID resolved by a data source, or an attribute that is immutable such as the availability zone, subnet or certain instance metadata options. Read the plan carefully: Terraform annotates the specific attribute with "forces replacement", which names the cause precisely. If it is an AMI refresh you did not intend, pin the AMI or add ignore_changes to the lifecycle block.
How do I attach an IAM role to an EC2 instance in Terraform?

Create an aws_iam_role with a trust policy allowing ec2.amazonaws.com, attach the permission policies, then create an aws_iam_instance_profile referencing the role and set iam_instance_profile on the instance or launch template. The instance profile is the piece people miss. An EC2 instance cannot reference a role directly, and forgetting it produces credentials errors inside the instance that look unrelated to Terraform.
How do I manage EBS volumes with Terraform?

The root volume is configured inline with a root_block_device block; additional volumes are separate aws_ebs_volume resources attached with aws_volume_attachment. Use gp3 rather than gp2, since it is cheaper and faster with performance independent of size. Set encrypted = true, or better, enable EBS encryption by default at the account level so no configuration can forget it. Note that additional volumes do not delete on termination by default, which is usually what you want but does leave orphans if instances are replaced often.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.

terraform-aws-ec2.markdown:
## Continuing the AWS Project In the previous lesson, you built the network layer: a custom VPC, public and private subnets, an internet gateway, route tables, and a NAT gateway. That network is the foundation. Now it is time to place a compute resource inside it. In this lesson, you will launch a **public EC2 web server** with Terraform. The finished setup includes: - a security group that allows HTTP and SSH - a data source that discovers the latest Ubuntu AMI - an EC2 instance in a public subnet - a `user_data` script that installs Nginx automatically - a key pair for SSH access - an Elastic IP so the instance keeps a stable public address - output values so you can quickly find the server after deployment This is a realistic next step because infrastructure projects rarely stop at âthe network exists.â A useful VPC normally hosts something: a web server, an application tier, a bastion host, or a load balancer. ## Architecture for This Lesson You are continuing from the VPC project, so the EC2 instance will launch into one of the public subnets created earlier. ```text Internet â Elastic IP â EC2 instance (Nginx) â Security Group (80, 22 open) â Public subnet â VPC ``` For a learning project, a public EC2 instance is convenient because it is easy to test from your browser and from SSH. In a production system, you would usually place application instances in private subnets behind a load balancer, but starting with a public demo host keeps the lesson focused. ## Prerequisites You should already have: - the VPC resources from the previous lesson - working AWS credentials - Terraform installed - an SSH public key on your machine, such as `~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub` or `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` You also need a private key that matches the public key you upload. Terraform creates the AWS key pair resource from the **public** key. SSH later uses the **private** key on your machine. ## Referencing the Existing VPC Resources Because this lesson continues the previous tutorial, the example below assumes these resources already exist in the same Terraform project: - `aws_vpc.main` - `aws_subnet.public` That means the EC2 resources can refer to them directly. If you later refactor your VPC into a separate module, the references would typically become module outputs such as `module.network.vpc_id` and `module.network.public_subnet_ids[0]`. ## Creating the Security Group The security group is the instance-level firewall. It decides which traffic is allowed in and out. ```hcl resource "aws_security_group" "web" { name = "${var.project_name}-web-sg" description = "Allow SSH and HTTP access to the web server" vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id ingress { description = "SSH" from_port = 22 to_port = 22 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = [var.ssh_allowed_cidr] } ingress { description = "HTTP" from_port = 80 to_port = 80 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } egress { from_port = 0 to_port = 0 protocol = "-1" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-web-sg" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } ``` ### Why separate SSH and HTTP rules? Because they serve different purposes: - SSH on port 22 is for administration - HTTP on port 80 is for application traffic It is tempting in a lab to open SSH to `0.0.0.0/0`, but that is not a good long-term habit. This tutorial uses a variable so you can scope SSH to your own IP or corporate network. ```hcl variable "ssh_allowed_cidr" { description = "CIDR allowed to SSH into the EC2 instance" type = string default = "203.0.113.10/32" } ``` Replace that example IP with your real source CIDR before applying. ## Finding the Latest Ubuntu AMI with a Data Source Hardcoding AMI IDs is a common beginner mistake. AMIs are region-specific and change over time. A data source solves that cleanly. ```hcl data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" { most_recent = true owners = ["099720109477"] filter { name = "name" values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd-gp3/ubuntu-noble-24.04-amd64-server-*"] } filter { name = "virtualization-type" values = ["hvm"] } } ``` ### What this does - `most_recent = true` asks AWS for the latest matching image - `owners = ["099720109477"]` restricts results to Canonical, the publisher of official Ubuntu AMIs - the `name` filter matches the Ubuntu release pattern - the virtualization filter avoids odd matches that are not normal HVM images This is far better than copying an AMI ID from a blog post. With the data source, the tutorial stays region-aware and less likely to go stale. ## Creating a Key Pair for SSH Access To SSH into the instance later, create an AWS key pair resource from your local public key file. ```hcl resource "aws_key_pair" "deployer" { key_name = "${var.project_name}-key" public_key = file(var.public_key_path) tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-key" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } ``` The important piece is `file(var.public_key_path)`. The `file()` function reads a local file and returns its contents as a string. Define the variable like this: ```hcl variable "public_key_path" { description = "Path to the SSH public key file" type = string default = "~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub" } ``` ### A practical note about `~` Some shells expand `~`, but Terraform itself does not always behave the way beginners expect with home-directory shortcuts. If you run into trouble, use the full absolute path instead. For example: ```hcl public_key_path = "/Users/yourname/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub" ``` ## Writing the User Data Script `user_data` lets you bootstrap the instance when it starts. Instead of SSHing in manually and installing Nginx yourself, Terraform passes a startup script to cloud-init on the VM. ```hcl locals { web_user_data = <<-EOF #!/bin/bash set -e apt-get update -y apt-get install -y nginx cat > /var/www/html/index.html <<'HTML' Terraform AWS Web Server

It works!

This EC2 instance was provisioned by Terraform.

HTML systemctl enable nginx systemctl restart nginx EOF } ``` ### Why user data matters This pattern keeps the infrastructure reproducible. If the instance is destroyed and recreated, it configures itself the same way every time. That is much better than âlaunch a VM and click around until it works.â It is also your first taste of the boundary between provisioning and configuration management: - Terraform provisions the server - the `user_data` script performs lightweight first-boot configuration For more advanced software configuration, tools like cloud-init, Packer, or Ansible are often cleaner than long user data scripts. ## Creating the EC2 Instance Now you can define the instance. ```hcl resource "aws_instance" "web" { ami = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id instance_type = var.instance_type subnet_id = aws_subnet.public[0].id vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id] key_name = aws_key_pair.deployer.key_name associate_public_ip_address = true user_data = local.web_user_data tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-web" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } ``` ### Important arguments explained - `ami` chooses the Ubuntu image from the data source - `instance_type` controls CPU and memory - `subnet_id` places the instance in the first public subnet - `vpc_security_group_ids` attaches the firewall rules - `key_name` links the uploaded AWS key pair - `associate_public_ip_address = true` is fine for this lab, though you will also attach an Elastic IP next - `user_data` installs Nginx automatically Define the instance type variable: ```hcl variable "instance_type" { description = "EC2 instance size" type = string default = "t3.micro" } ``` `t3.micro` is a reasonable default for a tutorial because it is cheap and capable enough for a demo web server. ## Adding an Elastic IP AWS can assign a public IP automatically when the instance launches, but that address may change if the instance is recreated. An **Elastic IP** gives you a stable public address that survives instance replacement if you re-associate it. ```hcl resource "aws_eip" "web" { domain = "vpc" tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-web-eip" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_eip_association" "web" { instance_id = aws_instance.web.id allocation_id = aws_eip.web.id } ``` ### Why use an Elastic IP in a tutorial? Because it makes testing easy: - your browser bookmark stays valid - your SSH command stays the same - output values stay useful after small rebuilds In production, many teams avoid direct EIPs on application instances and put a load balancer in front instead. But for a single demo server, an EIP is simple and practical. ## Output Values for the Instance Outputs make Terraform easier to consume after apply. ```hcl output "web_instance_id" { description = "ID of the EC2 web instance" value = aws_instance.web.id } output "web_public_ip" { description = "Elastic IP address for the web server" value = aws_eip.web.public_ip } output "web_public_dns" { description = "Public DNS name of the EC2 instance" value = aws_instance.web.public_dns } ``` Now after `terraform apply`, you can run: ```bash terraform output web_public_ip terraform output web_public_dns ``` That is much faster than clicking through the AWS console looking for the instance. ## Running the Plan and Apply If you are adding these resources to the same project as the VPC lesson, run: ```bash terraform init terraform plan ``` In the plan, review: - the selected AMI - the security group ports - the SSH CIDR range - the subnet placement - the user data presence - the Elastic IP resource and association Then apply: ```bash terraform apply ``` ## Testing the Deployment After apply completes, grab the Elastic IP: ```bash terraform output web_public_ip ``` ### Test in the browser Open: ```text http:// ``` You should see the HTML page created by the `user_data` script. ### Test with SSH Use the private key that matches the public key you uploaded: ```bash ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ubuntu@ ``` Once connected, verify Nginx is running: ```bash systemctl status nginx curl localhost ``` If Nginx is active and `curl localhost` returns the sample HTML, the bootstrap process worked. ## Common Troubleshooting Tips If the browser test fails, check these likely issues: ### 1. SSH works but HTTP does not The most common cause is a security group mistake. Confirm port 80 is open to `0.0.0.0/0`. ### 2. SSH does not work Check: - the private key matches the uploaded public key - the username is `ubuntu` for Ubuntu AMIs - your SSH CIDR allows your current public IP - the instance really has the Elastic IP attached ### 3. The instance starts but Nginx is missing Inspect cloud-init logs on the server: ```bash sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/cloud-init-output.log ``` This file often reveals package install or script syntax errors. ## Complete Working Code Below is a complete working example that extends the earlier VPC project. ### `main.tf` ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.6.0" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 5.0" } } } provider "aws" { region = var.aws_region } data "aws_availability_zones" "available" { state = "available" } data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" { most_recent = true owners = ["099720109477"] filter { name = "name" values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd-gp3/ubuntu-noble-24.04-amd64-server-*"] } filter { name = "virtualization-type" values = ["hvm"] } } locals { web_user_data = <<-EOF #!/bin/bash set -e apt-get update -y apt-get install -y nginx cat > /var/www/html/index.html <<'HTML' Terraform AWS Web Server

Terraform deployed this server

Nginx was installed automatically with user_data.

HTML systemctl enable nginx systemctl restart nginx EOF } resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = var.vpc_cidr enable_dns_support = true enable_dns_hostnames = true tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-vpc" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_internet_gateway" "main" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-igw" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_subnet" "public" { count = length(var.public_subnet_cidrs) vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id cidr_block = var.public_subnet_cidrs[count.index] availability_zone = data.aws_availability_zones.available.names[count.index] map_public_ip_on_launch = true tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-public-${count.index + 1}" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_route_table" "public" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id route { cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0" gateway_id = aws_internet_gateway.main.id } tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-public-rt" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_route_table_association" "public" { count = length(aws_subnet.public) subnet_id = aws_subnet.public[count.index].id route_table_id = aws_route_table.public.id } resource "aws_security_group" "web" { name = "${var.project_name}-web-sg" description = "Allow SSH and HTTP access to the web server" vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id ingress { description = "SSH" from_port = 22 to_port = 22 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = [var.ssh_allowed_cidr] } ingress { description = "HTTP" from_port = 80 to_port = 80 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } egress { from_port = 0 to_port = 0 protocol = "-1" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-web-sg" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_key_pair" "deployer" { key_name = "${var.project_name}-key" public_key = file(var.public_key_path) tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-key" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_instance" "web" { ami = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id instance_type = var.instance_type subnet_id = aws_subnet.public[0].id vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id] key_name = aws_key_pair.deployer.key_name associate_public_ip_address = true user_data = local.web_user_data tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-web" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_eip" "web" { domain = "vpc" tags = { Name = "${var.project_name}-web-eip" ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } resource "aws_eip_association" "web" { instance_id = aws_instance.web.id allocation_id = aws_eip.web.id } ``` ### `variables.tf` ```hcl variable "aws_region" { description = "AWS region for the infrastructure" type = string default = "us-east-1" } variable "project_name" { description = "Name used in resource tags" type = string default = "devopslesson" } variable "vpc_cidr" { description = "CIDR block for the VPC" type = string default = "10.0.0.0/16" } variable "public_subnet_cidrs" { description = "CIDR blocks for public subnets" type = list(string) default = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"] } variable "instance_type" { description = "EC2 instance size" type = string default = "t3.micro" } variable "public_key_path" { description = "Path to the SSH public key file" type = string } variable "ssh_allowed_cidr" { description = "CIDR allowed to SSH into the EC2 instance" type = string } ``` ### `outputs.tf` ```hcl output "web_instance_id" { description = "ID of the EC2 web instance" value = aws_instance.web.id } output "web_public_ip" { description = "Elastic IP address for the web server" value = aws_eip.web.public_ip } output "web_public_dns" { description = "Public DNS name of the EC2 instance" value = aws_instance.web.public_dns } ``` ### `terraform.tfvars` ```hcl public_key_path = "/Users/yourname/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub" ssh_allowed_cidr = "203.0.113.10/32" instance_type = "t3.micro" ``` ## Final Thoughts This lesson shows how Terraform moves from ânetworking existsâ to âa real workload is running.â You used a data source to stay current with AMIs, a security group to control traffic, user data to automate first-boot configuration, and an Elastic IP to give the server a stable identity. That is a strong baseline for many AWS labs. Next, you can add storage and static content to round out the project. ## Practice Questions --- ## Frequently Asked Questions **How do I avoid hardcoding an AMI ID in Terraform?** Use the `aws_ami` data source with owner and name filters plus `most_recent = true`, or read AWS's published SSM public parameters with the `aws_ssm_parameter` data source, `/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64` resolves the current Amazon Linux image. Both remove a value that goes stale and becomes a security liability. Note that a new AMI then triggers instance replacement, so pair this with a launch template and an Auto Scaling group if you want control over when that happens. **Should I create EC2 instances directly or use a launch template?** Use a launch template with an Auto Scaling group for anything that matters, even at a desired capacity of one. A bare `aws_instance` is a pet: if it fails, nothing replaces it, and every change risks manual repair. A launch template plus an Auto Scaling group makes replacement routine and gives you rolling updates via instance refresh. Reserve standalone instances for genuinely one-off or experimental work. **How do I pass startup configuration to an instance?** Through `user_data`, rendered with the `templatefile()` function so values can be interpolated from Terraform. Use `user_data_replace_on_change = true` if you want a change to the script to replace the instance, since by default a modified `user_data` does not affect a running instance. It only executes on first boot. For anything substantial, bake the configuration into an AMI with Packer instead, which makes instances start ready and shortens boot time. **Why does Terraform want to replace my instance when I only changed a tag?** It usually does not, and a replacement means something else changed. Most often the AMI ID resolved by a data source, or an attribute that is immutable such as the availability zone, subnet or certain instance metadata options. Read the plan carefully: Terraform annotates the specific attribute with "forces replacement", which names the cause precisely. If it is an AMI refresh you did not intend, pin the AMI or add `ignore_changes` to the lifecycle block. **How do I attach an IAM role to an EC2 instance in Terraform?** Create an `aws_iam_role` with a trust policy allowing `ec2.amazonaws.com`, attach the permission policies, then create an `aws_iam_instance_profile` referencing the role and set `iam_instance_profile` on the instance or launch template. The instance profile is the piece people miss. An EC2 instance cannot reference a role directly, and forgetting it produces credentials errors inside the instance that look unrelated to Terraform. **How do I manage EBS volumes with Terraform?** The root volume is configured inline with a `root_block_device` block; additional volumes are separate `aws_ebs_volume` resources attached with `aws_volume_attachment`. Use `gp3` rather than `gp2`, since it is cheaper and faster with performance independent of size. Set `encrypted = true`, or better, enable EBS encryption by default at the account level so no configuration can forget it. Note that additional volumes do not delete on termination by default, which is usually what you want but does leave orphans if instances are replaced often.

terraform-aws-s3.title: Terraform AWS S3 Static Assets
terraform-aws-s3.subtitle: Create an S3 bucket with Terraform: unique names with random_id, versioning, lifecycle rules, public access settings, a bucket policy and object uploads.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing Terraform AWS S3 Static Assets must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Terraform documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Terraform in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Create an S3 bucket with Terraform: unique names with random_id, versioning, lifecycle rules, public access settings, a bucket policy and object uploads.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Terraform.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create an S3 bucket with Terraform: unique names with random_id, versioning, lifecycle rules, public access settings, a bucket policy and object uploads.

sections.title: Continuing the AWS Project
paragraphs: So far, the project has a network layer and a public EC2 web server. The next useful component is object storage. In AWS, that means S3.

In this lesson, you will create an S3 bucket that stores static assets such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and downloads. The tutorial goes a bit further than “create a bucket” because real buckets need policy and lifecycle decisions too.
By the end, your S3 configuration will include:

This lesson intentionally uses a public static-asset pattern because it is easy to understand and test. In production, many teams prefer CloudFront in front of S3 instead of a directly public bucket, but learning the underlying S3 pieces is still valuable.

sections.title: Why S3 Belongs in This Project
paragraphs: An EC2 web server is good for dynamic pages or server-hosted apps, but it is inefficient to store every image, CSS file, or downloadable document on the instance itself. S3 is a better fit because it gives you:
Even if the EC2 server disappears, the bucket and its objects remain. That decoupling is one of the big operational wins of cloud architecture.

sections.title: The Bucket Naming Problem
paragraphs: S3 bucket names must be globally unique across AWS. That means a name like devopslesson-assets may already be taken by another account anywhere in the world.
Terraform solves this neatly with the random_id resource from the Random provider.
First, add the provider requirement:
Then create a suffix:
That generates a short hex value you can append to the bucket name.

sections.title: Creating the S3 Bucket
paragraphs: Now create the bucket itself.
This is intentionally simple. The bucket resource creates the container, but most of the real behavior comes from additional resources.

sections.title: Bucket Ownership Controls
paragraphs: Modern AWS S3 setups often use explicit ownership controls.

It helps ensure the bucket owner remains the preferred owner of uploaded objects, which avoids confusing access patterns later. In multi-account or multi-uploader environments, ownership rules matter a lot.
For a simple tutorial, you may not feel the impact immediately, but it is worth learning because modern S3 configuration is more explicit than older examples you may see online.

sections.title: Public Access Block Configuration
paragraphs: S3 public access settings confuse many beginners because they interact with both ACLs and bucket policies.

For this tutorial, the bucket should allow public read access through a bucket policy so static files can be served openly. That means the public access block cannot completely forbid public policies.
This is one of those cases where context matters. If you were building a private application bucket, you would likely lock these values down much harder.

codeBlock.code:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "assets" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.assets.id

  block_public_acls       = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  block_public_policy     = false
  restrict_public_buckets = false
}

sections.title: Enabling Bucket Versioning
paragraphs: Versioning is one of the most practical features in S3.
Because static assets change over time, and mistakes happen. Versioning helps when:
In production, versioning is often non-negotiable for important buckets.

sections.title: Adding Lifecycle Rules
paragraphs: Buckets can quietly grow forever if you never manage object age. Lifecycle rules help move old data to cheaper storage classes or expire it automatically.
This exact policy may or may not match a production use case, but it teaches an important idea: storage should be managed intentionally.
If your bucket stores immutable assets with long-term value, you might keep them much longer. If it stores build artifacts or temporary content, expiration could happen much sooner.

sections.title: Creating the Website Configuration
paragraphs: Because the lesson asks for a website endpoint, the bucket needs static website hosting configured.
This tells S3 how to behave when someone browses the bucket as a static website.
There are two common ways to serve files from S3:
The website configuration is what gives you the website-style endpoint.

sections.title: Writing the Bucket Policy
paragraphs: To allow public reads, create a bucket policy. Using aws_iam_policy_document makes the policy easier to read than hand-writing JSON strings.
Anyone on the internet can read objects in the bucket with s3:GetObject. They cannot upload, delete, or list all bucket settings. It is intentionally narrow.

Still, public buckets require care. For a production public website, CloudFront plus a private bucket is often a stronger pattern. Here, the tutorial keeps the moving parts small so you can clearly see how S3 policies work.

sections.title: Uploading Files with aws_s3_object
paragraphs: A bucket with no objects is not very exciting. Terraform can upload files directly.

For a tutorial, embedding content directly keeps the example self-contained. In larger projects, you will often prefer source = "path/to/file" so your real HTML, CSS, and image assets live as normal files in the repository.

sections.title: Outputting the Bucket Name and Website Endpoint
paragraphs: Outputs make post-apply testing simple.
Then open the endpoint in your browser.

sections.title: Running Plan and Apply
paragraphs: As always, initialize first if you added a new provider:
Review the plan carefully for:

codeBlock.code: terraform init

sections.title: Complete Working Code
paragraphs: Below is a complete working example for this S3 layer.

sections.title: A Practical Production Note
paragraphs: This tutorial makes the bucket public because the goal is to teach bucket policy, public access controls, and website hosting in one place. For production internet-facing sites, a stronger pattern is often:
Still, if you understand the simpler public bucket design first, the more secure production pattern becomes easier to reason about.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
paragraphs: The S3 part of the project teaches an important Terraform lesson: cloud resources are rarely “done” after the first resource block. Buckets need naming strategy, access design, versioning decisions, lifecycle management, and often object uploads or policies.
That is why Terraform is so useful. Instead of manually remembering every checkbox in the AWS console, you define the bucket once in code and recreate it consistently.

sections.title: Practice Questions
paragraphs: Why does this tutorial use a `random_id` resource when naming the S3 bucket?
Why does the tutorial set `block_public_policy = false` on the S3 public access block resource?
What is the main purpose of an S3 lifecycle configuration?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does my S3 bucket configuration need so many separate resources?

Because the AWS provider split what was once a set of inline blocks on aws_s3_bucket into standalone resources, aws_s3_bucket_versioning, aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration, aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration and others. Older tutorials showing versioning or encryption inline are written for the pre-v4 provider and will not work. Each setting is now its own resource referencing the bucket by ID.
How do I make a bucket private and keep it that way?

Create an aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block with all four settings true, which is a hard override that no bucket policy can bypass. Combine it with aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls set to BucketOwnerEnforced, which disables ACLs entirely. Object ACLs were behind most historic S3 exposure incidents. For content that genuinely must be public, front the private bucket with CloudFront using an Origin Access Control rather than opening the bucket.
How do I stop Terraform from deleting a bucket that contains objects?

By default AWS refuses to delete a non-empty bucket and the destroy fails, which is a useful accident. force_destroy = true makes Terraform empty it first, which is convenient for ephemeral test buckets and dangerous anywhere else. Set it deliberately and never on anything holding real data. For production, add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } so Terraform refuses any plan that would remove it.
How do I configure lifecycle rules in Terraform?

With aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration, containing rule blocks with transition and expiration actions. Add an abort_incomplete_multipart_upload rule to every bucket. Failed multipart uploads leave parts that are billed as storage but do not appear in a normal listing, and teams discover them years later as an unexplained cost. If versioning is enabled, include noncurrent_version_expiration or old versions accumulate indefinitely.
Should I use a bucket policy or IAM policies?

Within one account, IAM policies on the principals are sufficient and simpler. Use a bucket policy for cross-account access, for conditions that must apply to every caller regardless of their IAM, such as denying any request not over HTTPS, and for granting access to AWS services like CloudFront. A common mistake is writing both when only IAM is needed, which doubles the places a permission can be wrong.
How do I manage the S3 bucket that holds my Terraform state?

Not in the configuration that uses it, since the bucket must exist before terraform init can store state there. Create it in a small separate configuration with local state, or once via the CLI. Enable versioning so a bad state write can be recovered, enable encryption, block all public access, and restrict who can read it. State contains secrets in plain text. Keep that bootstrap configuration in version control even though its own state is local; it changes rarely.

Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
